Abduction–Deduction Entanglement:
Domain Generalization via Representation Transplants

Kasra Jalaldoust kasra@cs.columbia.edu Affiliation: Elias Bareinboim eb@cs.columbia.edu Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: Columbia University Affiliation: New York, NY 10027, USA
Abstract

Prediction models trained under the source distribution do not generalize well to a different target distribution. A valid inference about an unseen data distribution must be anchored by the invariance of certain causal mechanisms that generate the source and target data, however, these structural invariances are non-identifiable from the source data alone. Under mild causal assumptions about the data, we show that the optimal prediction in the target is in fact partially identifiable by the source distribution. The result rests on a simple observation: In any domain, the optimal prediction can be factorized into what we call a pair of abduction and deduction maps, where the abduction map makes inference about some unobserved variables (possibly confounders) from the observed variables and the deduction map predicts the label using both the observed and inferred quantities. Access to large source data pins down the optimal prediction, thus constrains the valid abduction–deduction ensembles that produce it — a non-identifiability that we call the abduction–deduction entanglement. To leverage this, we parameterize the constrained family using what we call a representation transplant, that is a specific linear transformation in the representation space that manipulates the abduction content of the representation while retaining the deduction component. Invariance of the causal mechanism generating the label implies existence of an invariant deduction map between source and target. Thus, we can search the space of plausible target distributions via a parametric transplant. We use this scheme in a learner–adversary game that, under an idealistic optimization, provably terminates with the learner having the minimax-optimal target prediction. Evaluations verify the theory, showing that the method is competitive in DG benchmarks.

1 Introduction

A prediction model trained on data from one distribution often degrades unexpectedly when the test distribution differs from the training one. From a learning-theoretic standpoint there is no a priori reason for it to be otherwise: without information relating source and target, no rule on the source controls the target risk (Ben-David et al., 2010). Challenges in domain generalization (DG) revolve around which structural assumptions are useful to bridge source and target domains while remaining plausible in modern ML applications.

Causal structural assumptions are promising inductive biases that allow principled probabilistic inference about unseen circumstances, and causal inference has inspired some of the important research directions on generalizability in machine learning. The driving principle in many of these work is that the statistical relationships between two data distributions are due to invariance of certain underlying causal mechanisms that generate the data. In the case of prediction, a favored assumption is that the label YY is generated by a causal mechanism that remains invariant, while the causal mechanisms that generate the covariates XX are subject to change. Under more restrictive assertions, such as absence of unobserved common causes (i.e., confounders), one can derive the invariant causal prediction principle (Peters et al., 2016): there exists a representation of covariates that learning to predict the label based on that representation yields a stable prediction across the domains. This inspires many of the work in DG that uses the heterogeneity in the source data to find invariant representations. Nonetheless, standardized DG benchmarks (Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz, 2021; Koh et al., 2021) indicate that under a uniform evaluation protocol, the existing methods do not consistently improve over vanilla ERM and the failure is partially due to a mismatch between the assumed structure and real-world generalization necessities. We argue that an alternative notion of invariance can be productive for domain generalization, without further structural assumptions; below is a motivating example.

1.1 A motivating example: moral questions and response prediction

Consider a passive Q&A panel: Subjective questions XX on different moral topics responded by individuals with different personalities UU, with binary responses Y∈{y0,y1}Y\in\{y_{0},y_{1}\} that represent action/inaction in a hypothetical scenario. The individuals answer to each question based on their moral values captured by U~:=ψ⁡(U)∈{−1,0,1}3\tilde{U}:=\psi(U)\in\{-1,0,1\}^{3}, a coarsening of the personality UU along three axes (Table 1), giving a total of |𝒰~|=27|\tilde{\mathcal{U}}|=27 different moral profiles.

For instance, consider the following question xx: “A scientist developing a drug that increases intelligence needs to test it on a volunteer who may suffer permanent mental impairment". The choices offered to the responder are y0y_{0}: “refuse to use the drug", and y1y_{1}: “use it.” A consequentialist person (u~1=+1\tilde{u}_{1}=+1), weighing the societal benefit of a working drug against one volunteer’s risk, may respond y1y_{1}; a deontologist (u~1=−1\tilde{u}_{1}=-1), holding that one must not use a person as a means to ends, is likely to respond y0y_{0}. Additionally, we know that each responder also has different tendencies regarding which questions they engage with: questions foregrounding freedom or pleasure attract more responses from individualists, while questions foregrounding duty or promises attract more responses from deontologist–collectivist individuals.

Suppose one uses this data and trains a prediction model to approximate P⁡(y1∣x)P(y_{1}\mid x). By the law of total probability, the model admits the following factorization:

P⁡(y1∣x)=∑u~∈𝒰~P⁡(u~∣x)⏟who might’ve responded to ​x​?⋅P⁡(y1∣x,u~)⏟what response would such a person give?P(y_{1}\mid x)\;=\;\sum_{\tilde{u}\in\tilde{\mathcal{U}}}\;\underbrace{P(\tilde{u}\mid x)}_{\text{who might've responded to }x\text{?}}\,\cdot\,\underbrace{P(y_{1}\mid x,\tilde{u})}_{\text{what response would such a person give?}} (1)

Any such prediction model can be viewed as an ensemble of two steps: an abduction P⁡(U~∣X)P(\tilde{U}\mid X) that infers the moral values of the question’s responder, and a deduction P⁡(Y~∣X,U~)P(\tilde{Y}\mid X,\tilde{U}) step that predicts what such an individual would respond. A familiar reader will recognize the same notion of abduction used in the 3-step counterfactual inference procedure—abduction, action, prediction (Pearl, 2009).

The factorization above is particularly useful to understand why a prediction fails under distribution shifts. For instance, in the moral questions example, it is likely that the abduction step “who might’ve responded to question xx” changes from one domain to the other; for instance, the change may be due to different moral value distributions across the populations, i.e., P​(U~)≠P⋆​(U~)P(\tilde{U})\neq P^{\star}(\tilde{U}), or a change in question–responder association, i.e., P⁡(X∣U~)≠P⋆​(X∣U~)P(X\mid\tilde{U})\neq P^{\star}(X\mid\tilde{U}), e.g., when in one population the individuals tend to engage with questions that challenges their views and in the other population individuals engage with questions even if it does not directly correspond to their moral stance.

Notice that the prediction rule P⁡(Y∣X)P(Y\mid X) is identifiable from the question/response data distribution P⁡(X,Y)P(X,Y). However, the true abduction and deduction remain unknown since for any random variable U~′\tilde{U}^{\prime} there exists a valid factorization with abduction P⁡(U~′∣X)P(\tilde{U}^{\prime}\mid X) and deduction P⁡(Y∣X,U~′)P(Y\mid X,\tilde{U}^{\prime}). The two factors, however, are not independent of each other: the ensemble must equal the prediction rule that is revealed by the data; we refer to this as the abduction–deduction entanglement. But how can an entanglement be useful for DG?

1.2 Existing remedy: eliminate the entanglement

A substantial line of work makes the DG problem tractable via structural assertions that remove the entanglement altogether. Invariant Causal Prediction (Peters et al., 2016) and Invariant Risk Minimization (Arjovsky et al., 2019) center around existence of a feature subset XI⊂XX_{I}\subset X such that optimal prediction based on it is invariant across source and target, P⁡(Y∣XI)=P⋆​(Y∣XI)P(Y\mid X_{I})=P^{\star}(Y\mid X_{I}); this is especially true for the direct causes of YY. The learning objective becomes identifying XIX_{I} from heterogeneous source data, e.g., diverse-enough domains or different interventional regimes. We defer a full discussion of this lineage to Section 4; here we read it through the abduction–deduction lens.

Relation to A/D.

Existence of an invariant predictor XI⊂XX_{I}\subset X is interesting from abduction–deduction point-of-view: It is equivalent to invariance of both abduction and deduction for any factorization, i.e., for all random variables U~′\tilde{U}^{\prime}, under some non-degeneracy assumptions11 1 Assuming that the equalities are not accidental, e.g., we exclude the cases where a mismatch between the abduction and deduction maps cancels out through marginalization; this notion is closely related to the notion of causal faithfulness (Spirtes et al., 2000; Pearl, 2009) widely employed throughout causal machine learning.,

P⁡(Y∣XI)=P⋆​(Y∣XI)⇔{P⁡(U~′∣XI)=P⋆​(U~′∣XI) (abduction invariance)P⁡(Y∣XI,U~′)=P⋆​(Y∣XI,U~′) (deduction invariance)P(Y\mid X_{I})=P^{\star}(Y\mid X_{I}){\iff}\begin{cases}P(\tilde{U}^{\prime}\mid X_{I})=P^{\star}(\tilde{U}^{\prime}\mid X_{I})&\text{ (abduction invariance)}\\ P(Y\mid X_{I},\tilde{U}^{\prime})=P^{\star}(Y\mid X_{I},\tilde{U}^{\prime})&\text{ (deduction invariance)}\end{cases} (2)

In words, causal assumptions that make invariant prediction viable are implicitly escaping the entanglement by making it idle. Not only this may not be viable (either practically, or even conceptually) in certain DG tasks of interest, but also invariance of both abduction and deduction may not be necessary for the source data to inform prediction in the target; we discuss how deduction invariance is enough. To make the deduction parameterization tractable, however, we need a representation that exposes the abduction and deduction factors as linear readouts—which leads us to the role of pretrained foundation representations.

1.3 Generalizability as a representation learning objective

Another important objective in unsupervised ML is to learn data representations that are useful for downstream tasks such as prediction/classification. Causal representation learning  (Schölkopf et al., 2021; Locatello et al., 2019; Hyvärinen and Morioka, 2016; Khemakhem et al., 2020; von Kügelgen et al., 2021; Ahuja et al., 2023; Brehmer et al., 2022; Squires et al., 2023; Lippe et al., 2022) aims to leverage data heterogeneity to identify the underlying causal variables and mechanism. The premise is that a “causal" representation captures changes to the data distribution in disentangled ways, and therefore, offers interpretability, robustness, and generalization for free to the downstream learner. In spirit, our discussion on abduction–deduction entanglement is related to the literature on disentangled representation learning, with a key distinction that we do not attempt to identify/disentangle the factors, rather use them to reason about a specified prediction task.

A complementary thread in modern ML attempts the same goal in downstream tasks by learning representations from large pooled datasets, a.k.a., the foundation models (Bommasani et al., 2021; Devlin et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020; Radford et al., 2021). The rationale is that a pretrained image/text representation ϕ:𝒳→ℝd\phi:\mathcal{X}\to\R^{d} that has been exposed to very large sets of diverse data from different domains would automatically develop the inductive biases that are necessary to generalize to unseen distributions.

Relation to A/D.

The foundation models perspective to learning generalizable representations is in fact sensible from the abduction–deduction perspective: Consider a moral question xx and a pretrained text embedding ϕ⁡(x)∈ℝd\phi(x)\in\R^{d}. Many different concepts related to question xx are captured by its representation, and empirical evidence suggests that these concepts are often linearly encoded in pretrained representations, a.k.a., the linear representation hypothesis (LRH)—tracing back to early evidence of arithmetic structure in word embeddings (Mikolov et al., 2013) and feature-direction findings in vision-model interpretability (Olah et al., 2020), and formalized as a named hypothesis by Park et al. (2024). If these concepts encoded in ϕ⁡(X)\phi(X), e.g., the realistic/idealistic framing of the question xx, happens to correlate well with the responder’s moral value U~\tilde{U}, then the representation contains the information necessary to mimic the true abduction rule, e.g., it is possible that P⁡(U~∣x)P(\tilde{U}\mid x) is linearly expressible in ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x). The LRH motivates—but does not formally imply—the softmax/sigmoid parameterization in Equations 6 and 7; the latter is our parametric working assumption, distinct from LRH as a phenomenon about pretrained representations.

1.4 Contribution

In this work, rather than removing entanglement, we embrace it; we parameterize the collection of abduction–deduction maps that are entangled by a source prediction. To make generalization viable, we assert invariant deduction, i.e., we assume that there exists some unobserved variable U~\tilde{U} for which P⁡(Y∣X,U~)=P⋆​(Y∣X,U~)P(Y\mid X,\tilde{U})=P^{\star}(Y\mid X,\tilde{U}), and to make matters tractable, we assume that the abduction/deduction maps for U~\tilde{U} are linearly encoded by ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x), inspired by the linear representation hypothesis. Notably, invariant deduction is readily derived from invariance of the causal mechanism for the label, i.e., fY​(X,U)=fY⋆​(X,U)f_{Y}(X,U)=f^{\star}_{Y}(X,U), provided the coarsening is sufficient for YY given XX—that is, P⁡(Y∣X,U)=P⁡(Y∣X,U~)P(Y\mid X,U)=P(Y\mid X,\tilde{U}), equivalently Y⟂U|X,U~Y\perp U\mid X,\tilde{U}. Under an arbitrary coarsening these can come apart, since marginalizing UU over the fiber ψ−1​(u~)\psi^{-1}(\tilde{u}) involves the domain-varying conditional Ps​(U∣X,U~)P^{s}(U\mid X,\tilde{U}). Invariance of fYf_{Y} is commonly assumed in many causality-inspired work in DG. Despite the non-identifiability, we show that the source distribution P⁡(X,Y)P(X,Y) partially identifies the target prediction P⋆​(Y∣X)P^{\star}(Y\mid X). For prediction in the target, we use a learner–adversary game called Causal Robust Optimization (CRO) whose solution attains the best worst-case target risk over causally plausible target distributions (Sections 2 and 3). Furthermore, we show that the existence of linear invariant representations (Arjovsky et al., 2019) emerges as a structural consequence—a corollary of the parameterization—rather than the learning principle. Empirically, CRO shows competitive results based on unified evaluation on some of the standard DG benchmarks in DomainBed (Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz, 2021). Most notably, on the diagnostic Colored MNIST cell where source and target color–label correlations are anti-aligned, CRO achieves 76%76\% target accuracy while the established and externally verified baselines—ERM, IRM (Arjovsky et al., 2019), GroupDRO (Sagawa et al., 2020), V-REx (Krueger et al., 2021), CORAL (Sun and Saenko, 2016), and Mixup (Zhang et al., 2018)—collapse to around 10%10\%. CRO also achieves competitive performance on real-world benchmarks (PACS, OfficeHome) where the deduction-invariance assumption is only approximate (Section 5).

1.5 Preliminaries and notation

We use uppercase ZZ to denote random variables, and lowercase zz to denote their values; the matching calligraphic letter denotes the set of possible values, e.g., x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}. We write P⁡(y1∣x)P(y_{1}\mid x) for P⁡(Y=1∣X=x)P(Y=1\mid X=x); softmax\mathrm{softmax}, sigmoid\mathrm{sigmoid} carry their standard definitions.

We work with structural causal models (SCMs) (Pearl, 2009) of the form,

U∼P⁡(u),X←fX​(U),Y←fY​(X,U).U\sim P(u),\quad X\leftarrow f_{X}(U),\quad Y\leftarrow f_{Y}(X,U).

where X,YX,Y are observable covariates and label, and UU is the unobserved common cause, a.k.a., the confounder. A coarsening of UU is any (typically discrete) variable U~:=ψ⁡(U)∈𝒰~\tilde{U}:=\psi(U)\in\tilde{\mathcal{U}}. In the multi-domain setting we observe X,YX,Y in KK source distributions P1,P2,…,PKP^{1},P^{2},\dots,P^{K}, and seek inference about an unseen target P⋆P^{\star}; in the appropriate context, P+P^{+} refers to pooled source distribution, i.e., P+​(x,y)=1K​∑s=1KPs​(x,y)P^{+}(x,y)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{s=1}^{K}P^{s}(x,y).

A predictor is g:=h∘ϕg:=h\circ\phi with ϕ:𝒳→ℝd\phi:\mathcal{X}\to\R^{d} being a fixed pretrained representation and h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H} a classification head that outputs class probabilities. The risk of gg under PP is denoted by RP​(g):=𝔼P⁡[ℓ⁡(g⁡(X),Y)]R_{P}(g):=\E_{P}[\ell(g(X),Y)], where ℓ\ell is a specified loss function. The running choice in this paper is the convex surrogate cross-entropy ℓ⁡(p^,y)=−log⁡p^y\ell(\hat{p},y)=-\log\hat{p}_{y}, used both in the algorithm and in our theoretical statements; we report 0​-​10\textnormal{-}1 accuracy as the evaluation metric.

2 Partial Transportability Result

This section develops the paper’s core machinery. We observe KK source distributions P1​(X,Y),…,PK​(X,Y)P^{1}(X,Y),\dots,P^{K}(X,Y) and seek to predict under an unseen target distribution P⋆​(X,Y)P^{\star}(X,Y) with small target risk RP⋆​(g):=𝔼P⋆⁡[ℓ⁡(g⁡(X),Y)]R_{P^{\star}}(g):=\E_{P^{\star}}[\ell(g(X),Y)]. Each domain induces the causal graph in Figure 1: X,YX,Y are observable, UU is an unobserved common cause of XX and YY, the response mechanism fYf_{Y} is shared across domains, and the cross-domain variation enters through a domain-specific prior πs​(U)\pi_{s}(U) over the unobserved UU. We work with a discrete coarsening U~:=ψ⁡(U)∈𝒰~\tilde{U}:=\psi(U)\in\tilde{\mathcal{U}} of the underlying UU, used to parameterize the abduction–deduction factorization below, and a frozen pretrained representation ϕ:𝒳→ℝd\phi:\mathcal{X}\to\R^{d}. Our construction has three parts: (i) an abduction–deduction factorization of the prediction rule into a domain-varying abduction map and a domain-invariant deduction map, parameterized as softmax/sigmoid readouts linear in ϕ\phi (softmax-linear abduction and logit-linear deduction); (ii) a low-rank linear operator on ϕ\phi—the cross-domain transplant—that swaps the abduction component of a representation across domains while preserving its deduction component; and (iii) a parameterized family of plausible target distributions derived from these two ingredients, against which we will optimize worst-case target risk in Section 3.

2.1 Illustrative example: domain generalization

Continuing the moral-questions example from Section 1: source data is collected from KK Q&A panels, each with its own prior πs​(U~)\pi_{s}(\tilde{U}) over the |𝒰~|=27|\tilde{\mathcal{U}}|=27 moral-values triples (Table 2); the target P⋆P^{\star} is an unrepresented panel whose composition we do not see. Concretely, three natural panels are a pragmatist panel concentrated on consequentialist–individualist–care individuals, an idealist panel concentrated on deontologist–collectivist–justice individuals, and a centrist panel concentrated on the balanced (mixed) corner. Each panel induces the causal graph of Figure 1; the response mechanism fYf_{Y} and the question library are shared, while the prior πs​(U~)\pi_{s}(\tilde{U}) varies across ss. Within each source ss, a sampled question XX is more likely to land on an individual whose U~\tilde{U} aligns with the panel’s mix, so the abduction map Ps​(u~∣x)P^{s}(\tilde{u}\mid x) varies with ss. Given the same question and the same U~\tilde{U}, however, the response is the same across panels—a consequentialist’s choice on a fixed question does not depend on which panel they were sampled from. Table 3 shows one representative scenario per panel. We return to this example throughout the section as an illustration; the development itself is in the abstract notation of Figure 1.

2.2 Abduction–deduction parameterization

For each domain s∈{1,…,K,⋆}s\in\{1,\dots,K,\star\}, the law of total probability decomposes the prediction rule into an inner product

Ps​(y∣x)=∑u~∈𝒰~Ps​(u~∣x)⋅Ps​(y∣x,u~),P^{s}(y\mid x)=\sum_{\tilde{u}\in\tilde{\mathcal{U}}}P^{s}(\tilde{u}\mid x)\cdot P^{s}(y\mid x,\tilde{u}), (3)

which we write as

Ps​(y1∣x)=P→s​(𝒖~∣x)⊤​P→s​(y1∣x,𝒖~).P^{s}(y_{1}\mid x)=\vec{P}^{s}(\bm{\tilde{u}}\mid x)^{\top}\,\vec{P}^{s}(y_{1}\mid x,\bm{\tilde{u}}). (4)
Definition 2.1 (Abduction and deduction maps).

For domain s∈{1,…,K,⋆}s\in\{1,\dots,K,\star\}, write both maps as rr-vectors indexed by u~∈𝒰~\tilde{u}\in\tilde{\mathcal{U}}:

P→s​(𝒖~∣x):=⟨Ps​(u~∣x)⟩u~∈𝒰~⊤(abduction map),\vec{P}^{s}(\bm{\tilde{u}}\mid x):=\langle P^{s}(\tilde{u}\mid x)\rangle_{\tilde{u}\in\tilde{\mathcal{U}}}^{\top}\qquad\text{(\emph{abduction map})},
P→s​(y1∣x,𝒖~):=⟨Ps​(y1∣x,u~)⟩u~∈𝒰~⊤(deduction map).\vec{P}^{s}(y_{1}\mid x,\bm{\tilde{u}}):=\langle P^{s}(y_{1}\mid x,\tilde{u})\rangle_{\tilde{u}\in\tilde{\mathcal{U}}}^{\top}\qquad\text{(\emph{deduction map})}.

The abduction map infers the unobserved U~\tilde{U} from the observed XX; the deduction map predicts YY given both XX and the inferred U~\tilde{U}, both under domain ss.

Within each domain, neither map is identifiable from data, but the two are entangled by Equation 4: their inner product is pinned to Ps​(y1∣x)P^{s}(y_{1}\mid x), which source data identifies.

Remark 2.2 (Abduction–deduction entanglement).

We refer to this constraint as the abduction–deduction entanglement: the inner product P→s​(𝐮~∣x)⊤​P→s​(y1∣x,𝐮~)\vec{P}^{s}(\bm{\tilde{u}}\mid x)^{\top}\vec{P}^{s}(y_{1}\mid x,\bm{\tilde{u}}) is pinned to Ps​(y1∣x)P^{s}(y_{1}\mid x) by Equation 4 while the two factors individually remain underdetermined. The paper’s central move (Section 2.5) is to parameterize, rather than break, this entanglement.

Shared deduction, varying abduction.

The structural premise of the multi-domain setting is that the deduction map is invariant across domains while the abduction map varies. Conditioning on both XX and U~\tilde{U} pins down the response mechanism uniformly across domains; what differs across domains is which U~\tilde{U} likely produced a given XX. Formally,

P→1​(y1∣x,𝒖~)=⋯=P→K​(y1∣x,𝒖~)=P→⋆​(y1∣x,𝒖~),\vec{P}^{1}(y_{1}\mid x,\bm{\tilde{u}})=\dots=\vec{P}^{K}(y_{1}\mid x,\bm{\tilde{u}})=\vec{P}^{\star}(y_{1}\mid x,\bm{\tilde{u}}), (5)

while the abduction map Ps​(u~∣x)P^{s}(\tilde{u}\mid x) remains domain-specific.

Softmax/sigmoid parameterization linear in ϕ\phi.

We parameterize the abduction map as a softmax (multinomial-logit) readout and the deduction map as a sigmoid (logit-linear, or log-odds linear) readout, both linear in a frozen pretrained representation ϕ:𝒳→ℝd\phi:\mathcal{X}\to\R^{d}. Fix a transplant dimension rr for the parameterized coarsening (identified with |𝒰~||\tilde{\mathcal{U}}|). The true support size of U~\tilde{U} is generally unknown, so rr is a modeling choice; Figure 4 below stress-tests sensitivity to rr. We posit matrices A1,…,AK,A⋆∈ℝd×rA_{1},\dots,A_{K},A_{\star}\in\R^{d\times r} and D∈ℝd×rD\in\R^{d\times r} such that for every s∈{1,…,K,⋆}s\in\{1,\dots,K,\star\},

P→s​(𝒖~∣x)\displaystyle\vec{P}^{s}(\bm{\tilde{u}}\mid x) ≈softmax⁡(As⊤​ϕ​(x)),\displaystyle\approx\mathrm{softmax}(A_{s}^{\top}\phi(x)), (6)
P→s​(y1∣x,𝒖~)\displaystyle\vec{P}^{s}(y_{1}\mid x,\bm{\tilde{u}}) ≈sigmoid⁡(D⊤​ϕ​(x)).\displaystyle\approx\mathrm{sigmoid}(D^{\top}\phi(x)). (7)

Indexing convention. Fix an ordering of 𝒰~\tilde{\mathcal{U}}. Both sides of Equations 6 and 7 are rr-vectors indexed by u~∈𝒰~\tilde{u}\in\tilde{\mathcal{U}}. The u~\tilde{u}-th entry on the LHS of Equation 6 is the scalar abduction probability Ps​(u~∣x)P^{s}(\tilde{u}\mid x); on the RHS, it is the u~\tilde{u}-th component of the softmax. For Equation 7, the u~\tilde{u}-th entry on the LHS is the scalar conditional Ps​(y1∣x,u~)P^{s}(y_{1}\mid x,\tilde{u}) (one Bernoulli probability per u~\tilde{u}); on the RHS, sigmoid\mathrm{sigmoid} is applied entry-wise to the rr-vector D⊤​ϕ​(x)D^{\top}\phi(x), and its u~\tilde{u}-th entry is the parameterized value of Ps​(y1∣x,u~)P^{s}(y_{1}\mid x,\tilde{u}). There is no u~\tilde{u} on the RHS as a variable; the u~\tilde{u}-dependence lives in the entry index.

AsA_{s} is the domain-ss abduction parameter and DD is the shared deduction parameter. The pair (As,D)(A_{s},D) parameterizes the abduction–deduction factorization as linear-in-ϕ\phi readouts under the softmax and sigmoid link functions. A trained head hs:ℝd→[0,1]h_{s}:\R^{d}\to[0,1] identified from domain-ss data, (hs∘ϕ)​(x)≈Ps​(y1∣x)(h_{s}\circ\phi)(x)\approx P^{s}(y_{1}\mid x), fixes the inner product in Equation 4 but leaves the factors (As,D)(A_{s},D) underdetermined. The entanglement is, in the parameterized form, an underdetermined system constraining (As,D)(A_{s},D) through hsh_{s}.

2.3 Representation Transplants

Definition 2.3 (Transplant basis).

Given abduction parameters A1,…,AK,A⋆∈ℝd×rA_{1},\dots,A_{K},A_{\star}\in\R^{d\times r} and deduction D∈ℝd×rD\in\R^{d\times r}, a transplant basis is any matrix L∈ℝd×rL\in\R^{d\times r} satisfying

As⊤L=Ir∀s∈{1,…,K,⋆},D⊤L=0.A_{s}^{\top}L=I_{r}\;\;\forall s\in\{1,\dots,K,\star\},\qquad D^{\top}L=0. (8)

A transplant basis simultaneously left-inverts every abduction map (including the unseen target’s) and lies in the left-null-space of the deduction map, so the transplant operator below acts only on the abduction component of ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x). Existence of LL is characterized in Proposition A.1 of Section A.1; d≥(K+2)​rd\geq(K+2)r is necessary, and generic-position parameters in such dd suffice.

Definition 2.4 (Transplant).

For s,s′∈{1,…,K,⋆}s,s^{\prime}\in\{1,\dots,K,\star\},

Ts→s′:W↦(Id+L⁡(As⊤−As′⊤))​W.T_{s\to s^{\prime}}:W\;\mapsto\;\big(I_{d}+L(A_{s}^{\top}-A_{s^{\prime}}^{\top})\big)\,W. (9)

The operator Ts→s′T_{s\to s^{\prime}} swaps the abduction component of a representation from what it is in domain ss to what it is in domain s′s^{\prime}, leaving the deduction component fixed; Section 4 discusses the relationship to linear-intervention operators on neural representations.

The transplant-basis conditions Equation 8 imply, for every W∈ℝdW\in\R^{d} and every s,s′∈{1,…,K,⋆}s,s^{\prime}\in\{1,\dots,K,\star\},

As′⊤​Ts→s′​W\displaystyle A_{s^{\prime}}^{\top}\,T_{s\to s^{\prime}}W =As⊤​W,\displaystyle=A_{s}^{\top}W, (10)
D⊤​Ts→s′​W\displaystyle D^{\top}\,T_{s\to s^{\prime}}W =D⊤​W.\displaystyle=D^{\top}W. (11)

The abduction reading at the transplanted vector matches the source-ss reading at the original vector, while the deduction reading is preserved (Lemma A.3 in Section A.2).

Prediction-invariance on transplanted inputs.

Take a point x0s∈suppPs⁡(X)x_{0}^{s}\in\supp_{P^{s}}(X) with representation w0s:=ϕ⁡(x0s)w_{0}^{s}:=\phi(x_{0}^{s}), set w0s′:=Ts→s′​w0sw_{0}^{s^{\prime}}:=T_{s\to s^{\prime}}\,w_{0}^{s}, and let x0s′∈ϕ−1​(w0s′)x_{0}^{s^{\prime}}\in\phi^{-1}(w_{0}^{s^{\prime}}) be a point whose representation matches. Assuming x0s′∈suppPs′⁡(X)x_{0}^{s^{\prime}}\in\supp_{P^{s^{\prime}}}(X), the transplant-basis conditions Equation 8 and the parameterizations Equations 6 and 7 imply

P→s′​(y1∣x0s′,𝒖~)\displaystyle\vec{P}^{s^{\prime}}(y_{1}\mid x_{0}^{s^{\prime}},\bm{\tilde{u}}) ≈sigmoid⁡(D⊤​w0s′)=sigmoid⁡(D⊤​ϕ​(x0s))≈P→s​(y1∣x0s,𝒖~),\displaystyle\approx\mathrm{sigmoid}(D^{\top}w_{0}^{s^{\prime}})=\mathrm{sigmoid}(D^{\top}\phi(x_{0}^{s}))\approx\vec{P}^{s}(y_{1}\mid x_{0}^{s},\bm{\tilde{u}}), (12)
P→s′​(𝒖~∣x0s′)\displaystyle\vec{P}^{s^{\prime}}(\bm{\tilde{u}}\mid x_{0}^{s^{\prime}}) ≈softmax⁡(As′⊤​w0s′)=softmax⁡(As⊤​ϕ​(x0s))≈P→s​(𝒖~∣x0s).\displaystyle\approx\mathrm{softmax}(A_{s^{\prime}}^{\top}w_{0}^{s^{\prime}})=\mathrm{softmax}(A_{s}^{\top}\phi(x_{0}^{s}))\approx\vec{P}^{s}(\bm{\tilde{u}}\mid x_{0}^{s}). (13)

By the abduction–deduction entanglement Equation 4 applied in each domain,

Ps​(y1∣x0s)\displaystyle P^{s}(y_{1}\mid x_{0}^{s}) =P→s​(𝒖~∣x0s)⊤​P→s​(y1∣x0s,𝒖~)\displaystyle=\vec{P}^{s}(\bm{\tilde{u}}\mid x_{0}^{s})^{\top}\vec{P}^{s}(y_{1}\mid x_{0}^{s},\bm{\tilde{u}})
=P→s′​(𝒖~∣x0s′)⊤​P→s′​(y1∣x0s′,𝒖~)=Ps′​(y1∣x0s′).\displaystyle=\vec{P}^{s^{\prime}}(\bm{\tilde{u}}\mid x_{0}^{s^{\prime}})^{\top}\vec{P}^{s^{\prime}}(y_{1}\mid x_{0}^{s^{\prime}},\bm{\tilde{u}})=P^{s^{\prime}}(y_{1}\mid x_{0}^{s^{\prime}}).

In words, transplanted points have invariant predictions across the domains they connect. The derivation requires the transplanted representation to admit a same-domain pre-image—a positivity-style condition we state formally as Assumption 3.6 in Section 3:

∀w∈ℝd:Ps​(ϕ⁡(X)=w)>0⇔Ps′​(ϕ⁡(X)=Ts→s′​w)>0.\forall w\in\R^{d}:\;\;P^{s}\big(\phi(X)=w\big)>0\;\;\iff\;\;P^{s^{\prime}}\big(\phi(X)=T_{s\to s^{\prime}}\,w\big)>0. (14)

The condition is enforceable across source pairs via a penalty, but for s′=⋆s^{\prime}=\star it is assumed (target XX is unobserved).

2.4 Invariant representations as a structural consequence

The transplant basis LL induces a decomposition of the representation into an abduction component (along LL) and a deduction component (orthogonal to LL). Pick any A∈ℝd×rA\in\R^{d\times r} with A⊤​L=IrA^{\top}L=I_{r} (any AsA_{s} from Equation 8 works). Then L​A⊤LA^{\top} is an oblique projector onto range⁡(L)\range(L), and

ϕ(X)=L​A⊤​ϕ​(X)⏟WA:abduction component+(Id−L​A⊤)​ϕ​(X)⏟WD:deduction component.\phi(X)\;=\;\underbrace{LA^{\top}\phi(X)}_{W_{A}:\ \text{abduction component}}\;+\;\underbrace{(I_{d}-LA^{\top})\phi(X)}_{W_{D}:\ \text{deduction component}}. (15)

The closure condition Equation 14 gives matched supports for Ps​(WA∣WD)P^{s}(W_{A}\mid W_{D}) and Ps′​(L⁡(As′⊤−As⊤)​WA∣WD)P^{s^{\prime}}(L(A_{s^{\prime}}^{\top}-A_{s}^{\top})W_{A}\mid W_{D}). Under a slightly stronger distributional-match condition—namely Ps​(WA∣WD)=Ps′​(WA∣WD∘Ts→s′)P^{s}(W_{A}\mid W_{D})=P^{s^{\prime}}\big(W_{A}\mid W_{D}\circ T_{s\to s^{\prime}}\big) across domains—the deduction component is an invariant representation. The derivation walks the law of total probability through a cross-domain identity and a fiberwise change of variables:

Ps​(y1∣wD)\displaystyle P^{s}(y_{1}\mid w_{D}) =∑wAPs​(y1∣W=wD+wA)​Ps​(wA∣wD)\displaystyle=\sum_{w_{A}}P^{s}(y_{1}\mid W=w_{D}+w_{A})\,P^{s}(w_{A}\mid w_{D}) (total probability)
=∑wAPs′​(y1∣W=Ts→s′​(wD+wA))​Ps​(wA∣wD)\displaystyle=\sum_{w_{A}}P^{s^{\prime}}\big(y_{1}\mid W=T_{s\to s^{\prime}}(w_{D}+w_{A})\big)\,P^{s}(w_{A}\mid w_{D}) (cross-domain identity)
=∑wA′Ps′​(y1∣W=wD+wA′)​Ps′​(wA′∣wD)\displaystyle=\sum_{w_{A}^{\prime}}P^{s^{\prime}}\big(y_{1}\mid W=w_{D}+w_{A}^{\prime}\big)\,P^{s^{\prime}}(w_{A}^{\prime}\mid w_{D}) (relabeling on the fiber)
=Ps′​(y1∣wD).\displaystyle=P^{s^{\prime}}(y_{1}\mid w_{D}).

The cross-domain identity is Ps​(y1∣W=w)=Ps′​(y1∣W=Ts→s′​w)P^{s}(y_{1}\mid W=w)=P^{s^{\prime}}(y_{1}\mid W=T_{s\to s^{\prime}}w) for ww in the source-ss support whose transplant lands in the source-s′s^{\prime} support, which follows from Equations 6 and 7 and the readout identities Equations 10 and 11 via softmax​(As⊤​w)⊤​sigmoid​(D⊤​w)=softmax​(As′⊤​Ts→s′​w)⊤​sigmoid​(D⊤​Ts→s′​w)\mathrm{softmax}(A_{s}^{\top}w)^{\top}\mathrm{sigmoid}(D^{\top}w)=\mathrm{softmax}(A_{s^{\prime}}^{\top}T_{s\to s^{\prime}}w)^{\top}\mathrm{sigmoid}(D^{\top}T_{s\to s^{\prime}}w) (see Lemma A.3 in the appendix). The relabeling step substitutes wA′:=πA​Ts→s′​(wD+wA)w_{A}^{\prime}:=\pi_{A}T_{s\to s^{\prime}}(w_{D}+w_{A}) with πA:=L​A⊤\pi_{A}:=LA^{\top} the projector onto the abduction component; under Assumption 3.2 this is a bijection of the (finite) WAW_{A}-fiber at fixed WD=wDW_{D}=w_{D}, and the mass relabeling matches Ps′​(wA′∣wD)P^{s^{\prime}}(w_{A}^{\prime}\mid w_{D}) by the distributional-match condition (see Remark A.5). The formal proof is in Section A.3. This calculation promotes to a corollary of the parameterization:

Corollary 2.5 (Invariant representation as a structural consequence).

Under the parameterization Equations 6 and 7 with shared deduction Equation 5, the transplant-basis conditions Equation 8, the closure condition Equation 14, and the distributional-match condition Ps​(WA∣WD)=Ps′​(WA∣WD∘Ts→s′)P^{s}(W_{A}\mid W_{D})=P^{s^{\prime}}(W_{A}\mid W_{D}\circ T_{s\to s^{\prime}}) across domains, the deduction component WD:=(Id−L​A⊤)​ϕ​(X)W_{D}:=(I_{d}-LA^{\top})\phi(X) (with AA any matrix satisfying A⊤​L=IrA^{\top}L=I_{r}, e.g. any AsA_{s}) is an invariant representation:

Ps(Y∣WD)=Ps′(Y∣WD),∀s,s′∈{1,…,K,⋆}.P^{s}(Y\mid W_{D})\;=\;P^{s^{\prime}}(Y\mid W_{D}),\qquad\forall s,s^{\prime}\in\{1,\dots,K,\star\}.

Existing work on invariance learning (Arjovsky et al., 2019) can be interpreted as attempts to directly recover this deduction component. We note, however, that the deduction component alone is non-identifiable and insufficient for prediction without re-coupling to an abduction; the invariance property here is a structural consequence of the abduction–deduction parameterization and closure under transplant, not an independent learning principle. Corollary 2.5 is not used by the algorithm in Section 3; it situates our parameterization relative to invariance-based DG. The next subsection turns the same machinery in the opposite direction, using the transplant to generate candidate target distributions rather than to extract an invariant representation.

2.5 Plausible-target family and surrogate risk

The ground-truth parameters A1,…,AK,A⋆,D,LA_{1},\dots,A_{K},A_{\star},D,L are not identified from observational source data alone. We treat them as parameters: tuples ({A~s},L~)(\{\tilde{A}_{s}\},\tilde{L}) with A~s⊤​L~=Ir\tilde{A}_{s}^{\top}\tilde{L}=I_{r} for every s∈{1,…,K,⋆}s\in\{1,\dots,K,\star\} and D⊤​L~=0D^{\top}\tilde{L}=0, together with parameterized transplants T~s→s′\tilde{T}_{s\to s^{\prime}} via Equation 9, produce a family of plausible target distributions, each consistent with the source-trained heads. Specifically, applying the same identity used in Equations 12 and 13 to the target,

P⋆​(y1∣X=x0⋆)=Ps​(y1∣X∈ϕ−1​(T⋆→s​ϕ​(x0⋆))),∀s∈{1,…,K},P^{\star}(y_{1}\mid X=x_{0}^{\star})=P^{s}\big(y_{1}\mid X\in\phi^{-1}(T_{\star\to s}\phi(x_{0}^{\star}))\big),\qquad\forall s\in\{1,\dots,K\}, (16)

which requires Equation 14 extended to the target. Equation 16 reads target-to-source: it ties a target prediction to a source prediction at the pre-image under T⋆→sT_{\star\to s}. The construction below uses the inverse direction, transplanting source representations into a target distribution; the two are related by Ts→⋆=T⋆→s−1T_{s\to\star}=T_{\star\to s}^{-1} (unipotence; Lemma A.3).

Closure penalty.

Closure across source pairs is enforceable from data. We penalize it via the Hausdorff distance between actual and transplanted source supports:

Closure⁡({A~s},L~):=∑s,s′∈{1,…,K}maxx∈suppPs⁡(X)⁡minx′∈suppPs′⁡(X)​‖ϕ⁡(x′)−T~s→s′​ϕ​(x)‖.\mathrm{Closure}(\{\tilde{A}_{s}\},\tilde{L}):=\sum_{s,s^{\prime}\in\{1,\dots,K\}}\max_{x\in\supp_{P^{s}}(X)}\min_{x^{\prime}\in\supp_{P^{s^{\prime}}}(X)}\big\|\phi(x^{\prime})-\tilde{T}_{s\to s^{\prime}}\phi(x)\big\|. (17)

Closure to the target regime cannot be enforced empirically because target XX is unobserved; it must be assumed.

Fit constraint.

For a candidate target head g~⋆:ℝd→[0,1]\tilde{g}^{\star}:\R^{d}\to[0,1] on top of the frozen ϕ\phi, Equation 16 ties source supports to target supports: g~⋆\tilde{g}^{\star} is consistent with ({A~s},L~)(\{\tilde{A}_{s}\},\tilde{L}) if it minimizes cross-entropy on transformed source data,

Fit(g~⋆,{A~s},L~):=∑s∈{1,…,K}𝔼X,Y∼Ps[CE(g~⋆(T~s→⋆ϕ(X)),Y)].\mathrm{Fit}(\tilde{g}^{\star},\{\tilde{A}_{s}\},\tilde{L}):=\sum_{s\in\{1,\dots,K\}}\E_{X,Y\sim P^{s}}\big[\mathrm{CE}\big(\tilde{g}^{\star}(\tilde{T}_{s\to\star}\phi(X)),Y\big)\big]. (18)
Surrogate target distribution and risk.

In standard DG the learner has no target data—not even unlabeled XX samples from P⋆​(X)P^{\star}(X)—so direct evaluation of target risk is unavailable. The transplant identity Equation 16 ties source supports to target supports, motivating evaluation on a surrogate P~⋆​(X,Y)=P~⋆​(X)⋅P⋆​(Y∣X)\tilde{P}^{\star}(X,Y)=\tilde{P}^{\star}(X)\cdot P^{\star}(Y\mid X) with suppP~⋆⁡(X)=suppP⋆⁡(X)\supp_{\tilde{P}^{\star}}(X)=\supp_{P^{\star}}(X). With discrete support and a complex-enough hypothesis class, arg​minh:𝒳→𝒴RP~⋆(h)=arg​minh:𝒳→𝒴RP⋆(h)\argmin_{h:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}}R_{\tilde{P}^{\star}}(h)=\argmin_{h:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}}R_{P^{\star}}(h), so minimizing surrogate risk is a valid proxy for minimizing target risk. A practical choice for P~⋆​(X)\tilde{P}^{\star}(X) is to apply transplant to source representations:

P~⋆​(ϕ​(x),y)\displaystyle\tilde{P}^{\star}(\phi(x),y) :=P~⋆​(ϕ⁡(x))⋅P⋆​(y1∣ϕ⁡(x))\displaystyle:=\tilde{P}^{\star}(\phi(x))\cdot P^{\star}(y_{1}\mid\phi(x))
=Ps(T~s→⋆ϕ(X))⋅g~⋆(T~s→⋆ϕ(X)).\displaystyle=P^{s}(\tilde{T}_{s\to\star}\phi(X))\cdot\tilde{g}^{\star}(\tilde{T}_{s\to\star}\phi(X)). (19)

This is consistent with Equation 18. The surrogate target risk of a classifier h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H} is then

Risk⁡(h,g~⋆,{A~s},L~):=𝔼W∼P~⋆​(ϕ⁡(X)),Y∼g~⋆​(W)⁡[ℓ⁡(h⁡(W),Y)].\mathrm{Risk}(h;\tilde{g}^{\star},\{\tilde{A}_{s}\},\tilde{L}):=\E_{W\sim\tilde{P}^{\star}(\phi(X)),\,Y\sim\tilde{g}^{\star}(W)}\big[\ell(h(W),Y)\big]. (20)

The two heads play distinct roles: g~⋆\tilde{g}^{\star} is the adversary’s candidate target head—part of the transplant parameterization (g~⋆,{A~s},L~)(\tilde{g}^{\star},\{\tilde{A}_{s}\},\tilde{L}) that synthesizes a plausible target (X,Y)(X,Y) distribution—while h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H} is the learner’s classifier evaluated against that synthesized distribution. The learner’s objective therefore depends on the adversary’s choice of head through P~⋆\tilde{P}^{\star}.

Best worst-case objective.

We upper-bound the surrogate target risk of a classifier hh by maximizing the risk while encouraging Fit\mathrm{Fit} optimality and penalizing Closure\mathrm{Closure}:

Obj⁡(g~⋆,{A~s},L~,h):=Risk⁡(h,g~⋆,{A~s},L~)−λ1⋅Fit⁡(g~⋆,{A~s},L~)−λ2⋅Closure⁡({A~s},L~),\mathrm{Obj}\big(\tilde{g}^{\star},\{\tilde{A}_{s}\},\tilde{L};h\big):=\mathrm{Risk}(h;\tilde{g}^{\star},\{\tilde{A}_{s}\},\tilde{L})-\lambda_{1}\cdot\mathrm{Fit}(\tilde{g}^{\star},\{\tilde{A}_{s}\},\tilde{L})-\lambda_{2}\cdot\mathrm{Closure}(\{\tilde{A}_{s}\},\tilde{L}), (21)

with λ1,λ2\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2} regularization hyperparameters controlling how strictly the theoretical constraints are imposed. We seek h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H} minimizing the surrogate-risk upper bound:

h⋆∈arg​minh∈ℋ⁡Risk​(h,arg​maxg~⋆,{A~s},L~⁡Obj​(g~⋆,{A~s},L~,h)).h^{\star}\;\in\;\argmin_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\;\mathrm{Risk}\big(h;\,\argmax_{\tilde{g}^{\star},\{\tilde{A}_{s}\},\tilde{L}}\mathrm{Obj}(\tilde{g}^{\star},\{\tilde{A}_{s}\},\tilde{L};h)\big). (22)

Section 3 presents an algorithm that solves this min-max optimization and a guarantee on its solution.

3 Algorithm and Guarantee

3.1 A learner–adversary game

The transplant parameterization of Section 2 yields, for any hh, an upper bound on the surrogate target risk by searching over abduction–deduction pairs consistent with the source distributions. To find h⋆h^{\star} minimizing this bound (Equation 22), we adapt the Causal Robust Optimization (CRO) algorithm of Jalaldoust et al. (2024): a game between a learner and an adversary in which, at iteration tt, the learner proposes a candidate ht∈ℋh_{t}\in\mathcal{H} and the adversary uses the transplant parameterization to find a hard plausible target distribution P^t⋆\hat{P}^{\star}_{t} on which hth_{t}’s risk is large. The learner adds P^t⋆\hat{P}^{\star}_{t} to a growing collection 𝒫^⋆={P^1⋆,…,P^t⋆}\hat{\mathcal{P}}^{\star}=\{\hat{P}^{\star}_{1},\dots,\hat{P}^{\star}_{t}\} and updates hth_{t} to minimize the maximum risk over the collection. The game terminates when this maximum risk converges. In practice we work with empirical distributions P^1,…,P^K\hat{P}^{1},\dots,\hat{P}^{K} and write Obj^\widehat{\mathrm{Obj}} for the plug-in estimator of Obj\mathrm{Obj}. Algorithm 1 gives the pseudocode.

The adversary step (line 4), at fixed ht−1h_{t-1}, bounds the surrogate target risk by maximizing over transplant parameters subject to the source-fit term Fit\mathrm{Fit} (Equation 18) and the closure penalty Closure\mathrm{Closure} (Equation 17). The learner step (line 6) refines hh to make this bound tight. The two steps together implement the min-max in Equation 22.

Frozen vs. refined predictors.

If hh is frozen at the initial pooled-source ERM and the outer learner step is omitted, CRO becomes a pure partial evaluation of target risk for that fixed predictor. Including the learner step refines hh to minimize that bound, yielding the minimax guarantee below. The two regimes share the transplant-parameterized adversary; they differ only in whether hh is fixed or updated.

3.2 Minimax optimality

The guarantee for CRO depends on the adversary’s search space matching the family of plausible target distributions. We collect the five structural and regularity conditions used in the theorem.

Assumption 3.1 (Confounded labels, multi-domain).

The source and target domains induce the causal graph in Figure 1.

Assumption 3.2 (Finite support).

YY is binary and XX has finite support.

Assumption 3.3 (Invariant deduction).

There exists a coarsening U~⊂U\tilde{U}\subset U such that P→s​(y1∣x,𝐮~)=P→s′​(y1∣x,𝐮~)\vec{P}^{s}(y_{1}\mid x,\bm{\tilde{u}})=\vec{P}^{s^{\prime}}(y_{1}\mid x,\bm{\tilde{u}}) for every x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} and s,s′∈{1,…,K,⋆}s,s^{\prime}\in\{1,\dots,K,\star\}.

Remark 3.4 (When fYf_{Y}-invariance gives Assumption 3.3).

Invariance of the structural label mechanism fYf_{Y}—i.e., Ps​(Y∣X,U)=Ps′​(Y∣X,U)P^{s}(Y\mid X,U)=P^{s^{\prime}}(Y\mid X,U)—implies Assumption 3.3 only when the coarsening is sufficient for YY given XX: P⁡(Y∣X,U)=P⁡(Y∣X,U~)P(Y\mid X,U)=P(Y\mid X,\tilde{U}), equivalently Y⟂U|X,U~Y\perp U\mid X,\tilde{U}. Without this sufficiency the within-fiber marginalization Ps(Y∣X,U~)=∑u:ψ⁡(u)=u~P(Y∣X,U=u)Ps(U∣X,U~)P^{s}(Y\mid X,\tilde{U})=\sum_{u:\psi(u)=\tilde{u}}P(Y\mid X,U=u)\,P^{s}(U\mid X,\tilde{U}) inherits the domain-varying πs\pi_{s} through Ps​(U∣X,U~)P^{s}(U\mid X,\tilde{U}), so fYf_{Y}-invariance and deduction invariance can come apart. Assumption 3.3 is stated directly on the coarsening to sidestep this subtlety.

Assumption 3.5 (Linear abduction–deduction, multi-domain).

There exist A1,…,AK,A⋆∈ℝd×rA_{1},\dots,A_{K},A_{\star}\in\R^{d\times r} (per-domain abduction parameters) and a single shared D∈ℝd×rD\in\R^{d\times r} (deduction parameter) such that for every s∈{1,…,K,⋆}s\in\{1,\dots,K,\star\} and every x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X},

P→s​(𝒖~∣x)=softmax⁡(As⊤​ϕ​(x)),P→s​(y1∣x,𝒖~)=sigmoid⁡(D⊤​ϕ​(x)),\vec{P}^{s}(\bm{\tilde{u}}\mid x)=\mathrm{softmax}(A_{s}^{\top}\phi(x)),\qquad\vec{P}^{s}(y_{1}\mid x,\bm{\tilde{u}})=\mathrm{sigmoid}(D^{\top}\phi(x)),

both read as rr-vectors indexed by u~∈𝒰~\tilde{u}\in\tilde{\mathcal{U}} in a fixed ordering, with sigmoid\mathrm{sigmoid} applied entry-wise.

Assumption 3.6 (Closure under transplant, multi-domain).

There exists L∈ℝd×rL\in\R^{d\times r} with As⊤​L=IrA_{s}^{\top}L=I_{r} for every s∈{1,…,K,⋆}s\in\{1,\dots,K,\star\} and D⊤​L=0D^{\top}L=0, such that for every s,s′∈{1,…,K,⋆}s,s^{\prime}\in\{1,\dots,K,\star\},

∀w∈ℝd:Ps​(ϕ⁡(X)=w)>0⇔Ps′​(ϕ⁡(X)=Ts→s′​w)>0.\forall w\in\R^{d}:\;\;P^{s}\big(\phi(X)=w\big)>0\;\iff\;P^{s^{\prime}}\big(\phi(X)=T_{s\to s^{\prime}}\,w\big)>0.
Theorem 3.7 (Minimax-optimality of CRO over the plausible target set).

Suppose access to infinite source data, i.e., perfect samplers for P1​(X,Y),…,PK​(X,Y)P^{1}(X,Y),\dots,P^{K}(X,Y), and that each gradient-based search in CRO (Algorithm 1) attains its global optimum. Under Assumptions 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.5 and 3.6, CRO terminates in finitely many iterations for every tolerance ϵ>0\epsilon>0, and the worst-case target risk of the returned classifier h⋆∈ℋh^{\star}\in\mathcal{H}—measured over the plausible target set entailed by the structural assumptions—converges to the minimax value as ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0:

maxP~⋆∈𝒫⋆​(P1,…,PK)⁡RP~⋆​(h⋆)→ϵ→0minh∈ℋ⁡maxP~⋆∈𝒫⋆​(P1,…,PK)​RP~⋆​(h),\max_{\tilde{P}^{\star}\in\mathcal{P}^{\star}(P^{1},\dots,P^{K})}R_{\tilde{P}^{\star}}(h^{\star})\;\xrightarrow{\epsilon\to 0}\;\min_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\;\max_{\tilde{P}^{\star}\in\mathcal{P}^{\star}(P^{1},\dots,P^{K})}R_{\tilde{P}^{\star}}(h),

where 𝒫⋆​(P1,…,PK)\mathcal{P}^{\star}(P^{1},\dots,P^{K}) is the set of target distributions entailed by any (K+1)(K+1)-tuple of SCMs compatible with Assumptions 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.5 and 3.6.

The proof, deferred to Section A.6, follows from the partial-transportability identity Equation 16 together with the convergence argument adapted from Jalaldoust et al. (2024). The statement is best read as a conditional guarantee: if the structural assumptions Assumptions 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.5 and 3.6 hold, CRO is minimax-optimal over the parameterized plausible set; the guarantee does not claim DG optimality outside this set.

Remark 3.8 (Target-side closure is not empirically verifiable).

The target component of Assumption 3.6 (at s′=⋆s^{\prime}=\star) is structural, not statistical: target XX is unobserved, so the empirical Hausdorff penalty (Equation 17) enforces closure only across source pairs. The conclusion of Theorem 3.7 is therefore conditional on target-side closure as an assumption rather than as a tested condition; we return to this caveat in the limitations.

Role of the assumptions.

The five assumptions divide as follows. Assumptions 3.1 and 3.3 are structural: the same confounded X→YX\to Y mechanism across domains, with deduction held invariant. Assumption 3.2 is a technical regularity. Assumption 3.5 is the parameterization choice—softmax-linear abduction and logit-linear (shared-DD) deduction in the pretrained representation space, which is what makes a small set of (As,D,L)(A_{s},D,L) parameters expressive. Assumption 3.6 is the load-bearing positivity-style condition: every transplant has a same-domain pre-image, including across the (unseen) target. The penalty in Equation 17 enforces a finite-sample analog of closure across source pairs only; closure to the target regime is assumed.

3.3 Robustness and finite-sample considerations

Theorem 3.7 is an asymptotic statement over a structurally idealized set: infinite source data, exact closure, and a global oracle for the inner searches. Two natural concerns are how the guarantee degrades when (i) closure holds only approximately—the unverifiable target-side condition of Remark 3.8—and (ii) source data is finite. We address each with a short statement; full proofs are in Section A.8.

Definition 3.9 (ϵ\epsilon-relaxed closure).

For ϵ≥0\epsilon\geq 0, the ϵ\epsilon-relaxed version of Assumption 3.6 requires the following: for every s,s′∈{1,…,K,⋆}s,s^{\prime}\in\{1,\dots,K,\star\} and every w∈ℝdw\in\R^{d} with Ps​(ϕ⁡(X)=w)>0P^{s}(\phi(X)=w)>0, there exists w′∈ℝdw^{\prime}\in\R^{d} with Ps′​(ϕ⁡(X)=w′)>0P^{s^{\prime}}(\phi(X)=w^{\prime})>0 and ‖w′−Ts→s′​w‖≤ϵ\|w^{\prime}-T_{s\to s^{\prime}}w\|\leq\epsilon, and symmetrically with s,s′s,s^{\prime} swapped. Exact closure is the case ϵ=0\epsilon=0.

Let 𝒫ϵ⋆\mathcal{P}^{\star}_{\epsilon} denote the plausible target set under ϵ\epsilon-relaxed closure (Assumption 3.6 replaced by Definition 3.9), and let Vϵ⋆:=minh∈ℋ⁡maxP~⋆∈𝒫ϵ⋆​RP~⋆​(h)V^{\star}_{\epsilon}:=\min_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\max_{\tilde{P}^{\star}\in\mathcal{P}^{\star}_{\epsilon}}R_{\tilde{P}^{\star}}(h) be its minimax value. Since the relaxed condition admits a strict superset of distributions (𝒫0⋆⊆𝒫ϵ⋆\mathcal{P}^{\star}_{0}\subseteq\mathcal{P}^{\star}_{\epsilon}), Vϵ⋆≥V0⋆V^{\star}_{\epsilon}\geq V^{\star}_{0}. The next theorem bounds the gap.

Theorem 3.10 (Graceful degradation under approximate closure).

Suppose Assumptions 3.1, 3.2, 3.3 and 3.5 hold, and that ℋ\mathcal{H} consists of LhL_{h}-Lipschitz heads h:ℝd→[δ,1−δ]h:\R^{d}\to[\delta,1-\delta] for some δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2); the loss is cross-entropy. Then

0≤Vϵ⋆−V0⋆≤Lhδ⋅ϵ.0\;\leq\;V^{\star}_{\epsilon}-V^{\star}_{0}\;\leq\;\frac{L_{h}}{\delta}\cdot\epsilon. (23)

The bound is linear in the closure residual ϵ\epsilon, so CRO’s worst-case target risk degrades smoothly rather than catastrophically as closure fails. The constant Lh/δL_{h}/\delta surfaces the two practitioner-facing knobs: head Lipschitzness on the representation space, and a confidence floor that keeps cross-entropy away from its singularity. The proof, in Section A.8.1, couples each “relaxed-closure” transplant target to an exact-closure one within ℓ2\ell^{2}-distance ϵ\epsilon and propagates through the loss.

Finite-sample plug-in error.

The minimax-optimality of Theorem 3.7 assumes infinite source data; the algorithm in practice uses empirical P^s\hat{P}^{s} with NN samples per source. A uniform-convergence argument over the (compact) parameter space ΘB\Theta_{B} of Step 3 of the Theorem 3.7 proof gives the following.

Proposition 3.11 (Finite-sample plug-in error, informal).

Let h^\hat{h} be the output of Algorithm 1 run on empirical P^1,…,P^K\hat{P}^{1},\dots,\hat{P}^{K} of size NN per source, and let ΘB\Theta_{B} be the parameter space of Step 3 of the Theorem 3.7 proof, with metric entropy log⁡𝒩⁡(ΘB,η)\log\mathcal{N}(\Theta_{B},\eta) at scale η\eta. Under Assumptions 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.5 and 3.6, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

maxP~⋆∈𝒫⋆⁡RP~⋆​(h^)≤V0⋆+C1​log⁡𝒩⁡(ΘB,η)+log⁡(1/δ)N⏟statistical error+ϵopt⏟optimization+ϵHaus⏟closure residual+η,\max_{\tilde{P}^{\star}\in\mathcal{P}^{\star}}R_{\tilde{P}^{\star}}(\hat{h})\;\leq\;V^{\star}_{0}\;+\;\underbrace{C_{1}\sqrt{\frac{\log\mathcal{N}(\Theta_{B},\eta)+\log(1/\delta)}{N}}}_{\text{statistical error}}\;+\;\underbrace{\epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}}_{\text{optimization}}\;+\;\underbrace{\epsilon_{\mathrm{Haus}}}_{\text{closure residual}}\;+\;\eta, (24)

for an absolute constant C1C_{1} depending on the cross-entropy Lipschitz constant 1/δ1/\delta and the operator-norm bound BB in (P1), where ϵopt\epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}} absorbs the suboptimality of the inner adversary and learner searches relative to their global optima, and ϵHaus=Closure⁡(A^s,L^)\epsilon_{\mathrm{Haus}}=\mathrm{Closure}(\hat{A}_{s},\hat{L}) is the residual empirical Hausdorff penalty at the returned parameters.

The statement names the three terms a practitioner can read off the algorithm’s outputs: a 1/N1/\sqrt{N} statistical rate (with log⁡𝒩⁡(ΘB,η)\log\mathcal{N}(\Theta_{B},\eta) playing the role of effective complexity), an optimization error governed by the global-optimum gap of the inner searches (zero under the assumption of Theorem 3.7, but typically positive in practice), and the source-pair Hausdorff residual that the algorithm minimizes during training. Tight constants for the softmax/sigmoid-linear-in-ϕ\phi class via bracketing entropy are standard and orthogonal to the paper’s contribution; we defer them to future work.

4 Related Work

We situate representation transplant and CRO with respect to four lines of prior work: causality-inspired domain generalization, distributional robustness, transportability and partial transportability, and linear interventions on neural representations. The transplant parameterization sits at their intersection: a linear operator on a frozen representation (lineage four) used as a primitive for partial transportability (lineage three) and operationalized via a learner–adversary game for worst-case DG (lineages one and two).

Causality-inspired domain generalization.

Causality-inspired DG methods build on related principles under different assumptions. Invariant prediction (Peters et al., 2016) establishes structural conditions under which heterogeneous data partially identify the causal parents of YY among covariates X=(X1,…,Xd)X=(X_{1},\dots,X_{d}), leveraging the invariance of source-prediction rules based on causal parents; Rojas-Carulla et al. (2018) extend this principle to causal transfer; IRM (Arjovsky et al., 2019) and V-REx (Krueger et al., 2021) operationalize related principles as regularized learning objectives. DomainBed-style empirical evaluations (Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz, 2021), however, have not validated meaningful gains over ERM, and the theoretical claims rely on assumptions—in particular the absence of unobserved confounding of YY—that may not hold. Our setting differs by treating the X→YX\to Y mechanism as confounded by U~\tilde{U} and parameterizing the resulting non-identifiability via the abduction–deduction factorization (Section 2); this is structurally distinct from a parents-of-YY recovery target. Corollary 2.5 recovers an invariant representation as a consequence of our parameterization rather than as a primitive learning goal.

Robustness and worst-case generalization.

Distributional robustness reformulates DG as a min-max over a family of distributions: Group DRO (Sagawa et al., 2020) optimizes worst-case risk over annotated subgroups. CRO (Algorithm 1) is a min-max of similar shape, but the family ranged over is structurally derived—the transplant-parameterized set of plausible targets entailed by source data and Assumptions 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.5 and 3.6—rather than user-specified or annotation-driven. On the evaluation side, WILDS (Koh et al., 2021) curates real-world distribution-shift benchmarks that complement the DomainBed protocol (Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz, 2021) used here.

Transportability and partial transportability.

The transportability literature (Pearl and Bareinboim, 2011; Bareinboim and Pearl, 2016) formalizes when causal effects estimated in a source population transfer to a target. Partial transportability (Lee et al., 2019; Jalaldoust et al., 2024) addresses settings where transfer is not point-determined but admits informative bounds; the multi-domain construction in Section 2 is most directly an instance of partial transportability of P⋆​(Y∣X)P^{\star}(Y\mid X), with the transplant operator providing a concrete parameterization on a pretrained representation.

Linear interventions on neural representations.

Mechanically, representation transplant is a low-rank linear intervention on a frozen pretrained representation, parameterized by ({As},L)(\{A_{s}\},L). Linear interventions on internal NN representations have a substantial recent history: interchange interventions for testing causal abstractions (Geiger et al., 2021) and their extension to interchange intervention training (Geiger et al., 2022); Distributed Alignment Search (DAS) (Geiger et al., 2024), which aligns interpretable causal variables with distributed subspaces of a frozen representation; activation patching for localizing factual knowledge (Meng et al., 2022); representation finetuning (LoReFT) (Wu et al., 2024) for parameter-efficient adaptation; activation steering (Turner et al., 2023) and representation engineering (Zou et al., 2023) for behavioral control; and concept erasure (INLP, R-LACE, LEACE) (Ravfogel et al., 2020; Ravfogel et al., 2022; Belrose et al., 2023) via learned linear projectors. Our construction is mechanically a member of this broader family. To the best of our knowledge, the most similar concept to our representation transplant is DAS (Geiger et al., 2024), together with its representation-finetuning extension LoReFT (Wu et al., 2024): DAS shares the counterfactual-style interpretation of a low-rank linear operator on a frozen ϕ⁡(X)\phi(X)—asking what the model would predict if a high-level causal variable were swapped via a representation-level interchange—but is deployed for mechanistic interpretability (verifying that an interpretable causal variable is aligned with a subspace of the representation), whereas our transplant is deployed for partial transportability and minimax DG. We adopt the same operator family for a different purpose—as a parameterization of the abduction–deduction non-identifiability of a trained predictor—and use it as a primitive for partial transportability and minimax DG. To our knowledge, no prior work uses linear-intervention operators for these targets, nor formalizes a closure-under-intervention assumption of the kind in Assumption 3.6.

5 Experiments

We evaluate Causal Robust Optimization (CRO; Algorithm 1) on a designed synthetic benchmark (Colored MNIST) and two real-world benchmarks (PACS, OfficeHome), and close with an empirical pass over the four structural premises that underlie the minimax guarantee. All evaluation follows the DomainBed protocol of Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz (2021): leave-one-environment-out cells, three random seeds per cell, identical hyperparameter budgets across methods, and training-domain validation as the model-selection rule. Source-validation accuracy is the only selection rule we report—target labels are never observed during model selection on any benchmark.

5.1 Implementation details

CRO is implemented on top of the DomainBed framework (Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz, 2021) as a new Algorithm subclass; baselines use the official DomainBed implementations. The featurizer ϕ\phi is ResNet-50 pretrained on ImageNet with AugMix for the image benchmarks (PACS, OfficeHome) and the standard 4-layer MNIST_CNN of DomainBed for Colored MNIST; in both cases the final classification head hh is a linear layer on top of frozen ϕ\phi. Training proceeds in two phases: Phase 1 is standard ERM-style training of (ϕ,h)(\phi,h) on the union of source domains; Phase 2 is the CRO outer loop (Algorithm 1) refining hh against the transplant-parameterized adversary. Per benchmark we sample 20 hyperparameter configurations ×\times 3 trial seeds (180 runs on Colored MNIST, 240 on each of PACS, OfficeHome) and select per cell by source-validation accuracy. Full architecture, two-phase training schedule, hyperparameter search ranges and per-dataset compute tiers, dataset statistics, GPU/wall-clock budgets, and reproducibility identifiers are documented in Appendix B.

5.2 Synthetic data: Colored MNIST

Task.

Colored MNIST (Arjovsky et al., 2019) is a binary classification of MNIST digits (Y=0Y=0 for digits 00–44, Y=1Y=1 for digits 55–99) where each image is colorized red or green according to a domain-specific correlation ρs\rho_{s} with the label. The source environments correspond to ρ=+0.9\rho=+0.9 and ρ=+0.8\rho=+0.8 (color tracks the label); the diagnostic environment is ρ=−0.9\rho=-0.9 (color anti-tracks the label). Color is a spurious feature whose label-correlation flips between source and target; shape is the invariant feature. The benchmark therefore isolates whether a method picks up the invariant structure when it is in tension with the spurious one—a designed instance of the shortcut-learning phenomenon documented across real-world DG benchmarks (Geirhos et al., 2020; Beery et al., 2018).

Source vs. target risk.

Before reporting benchmark numbers, it is informative to look at how source-validation risk relates to held-out target risk across CRO checkpoints. Figure 3 plots this relationship across the three Colored MNIST leave-one-out cells. The +90%+90\% and +80%+80\% cells (blue, magenta) lie close to y=xy=x: source-validation is a tight proxy for target performance. The −90%-90\% cell (orange) is the contrast—at source risk ≈0.35\approx 0.35–0.420.42, many checkpoints achieve target risk ≈0.22\approx 0.22–0.300.30, far below where the diagonal would put them, and the spread at fixed source risk is wide. The diagnostic cell is therefore exactly where source-validation is a poor proxy for held-out generalization, and is where standard ERM-style baselines that select by source-validation collapse in Table 4.

Results.

Table 4 reports leave-one-environment-out test accuracy under training-domain validation. Baseline numbers are reproduced from the DomainBed reference table (Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz, 2021); CRO numbers are our runs averaged over three seeds.

Discussion.

The −90%-90\% column is the diagnostic. All prior baselines collapse to ≈10%\approx 10\% accuracy (worse than chance): they inherit the source’s color–label rule and apply it to a target where that rule is inverted, so source-validation selects a predictor that is systematically wrong on the held-out cell. CRO at 76.0%76.0\% indicates the transplant-parameterized adversary surfaces an abduction–deduction factorization in which color sits in the abduction subspace (the LL-direction) and shape in the deduction subspace, with the learner converging onto the deduction readout. On the two source-tracking cells CRO matches the baseline cluster (72.1%/72.4%72.1\%/72.4\%); the per-column wins of ARM (82.0%/76.5%82.0\%/76.5\%) on those cells reflect its ability to absorb the source-side color correlation, which is exactly the rule that gets inverted on the diagnostic cell.

Stress test: transplant dimension.

The transplant dimension rr is the size of the parameterized coarsening of U~\tilde{U} (Equations 6 and 7). The true support size |𝒰~||\tilde{\mathcal{U}}| is generally unknown, so we stress-test sensitivity to rr on Colored MNIST: Figure 4 sweeps rr from 11 to the feature dimension 128128 and reports CRO target risk on all three leave-one-out cells. The two source-tracking cells (+90%+90\%, +80%+80\%) are flat in rr at target risk ≈0.28\approx 0.28–0.300.30. The diagnostic −90%-90\% cell is flat-low (≈0.23\approx 0.23) for r≤113r\leq 113 and then climbs sharply, reaching target risk ≈0.9\approx 0.9 at r=128r=128. The collapse beyond r≈113r\approx 113 happens because the orthogonal subspace L⟂L^{\perp}—the deduction component of ϕ\phi—becomes too small to carry an accurate invariant deduction map, so the worst-case risk on the diagnostic target explodes. The other two held-out cells do not collapse: at large rr, even with a poor deduction component the abduction component can compensate to fit the source predictions, and on a target whose abduction is well-aligned with the sources, the ensemble prediction remains good. Small to moderate rr avoids both failure modes and is the operating point we use for the headline numbers in Table 4.

CRO termination.

CRO (Algorithm 1) terminates when the worst-case risk over the growing collection of plausible targets stops increasing materially. Figure 5 reports the empirical distribution of iteration counts at termination across seeds and hyperparameter configurations. The diagnostic −90%-90\% cell terminates fastest (mode ≈4\approx 4, almost all mass between 33 and 66): the adversary identifies a small number of worst-case targets very quickly, and the learner converges to a worst-case-optimal predictor without needing many rounds. The source-tracking cells take a few more rounds (mode ≈7\approx 7 for +90%+90\%, bimodal at 44 and 66 for +80%+80\%), consistent with a less peaked worst-case landscape. Across the full sweep, termination occurs in at most 1313 outer iterations, so CRO’s compute budget is driven by the inner adversary and learner updates rather than the outer loop count.

5.3 Real-world datasets: PACS and OfficeHome

The two real-world benchmarks test CRO in regimes where the deduction-invariance assumption is at best approximate—rendering style and category-level appearance can themselves vary across domains, partially shifting the deduction map. We report numbers under the same DomainBed training-domain-validation protocol and analyze where CRO matches, leads, or trails strong baselines.

PACS.

PACS (Li et al., 2017) is a four-domain object-recognition benchmark (photo, art-painting, cartoon, sketch) with seven classes. Spurious features are texture and rendering style; the invariant features are object shape and category-level structure. Each cell holds out one of the four domains and trains on the other three.

Unlike on Colored MNIST, no baseline collapses on PACS, and CRO does not lead the average—SagNet (86.386.3) and CORAL (86.286.2) sit at the top, with CRO at 84.684.6 in line with the broad baseline cluster, leading Cartoon (81.081.0) and matching the Photo cluster (97.597.5, within 0.10.1 of the Mixup/RSC tie at 97.697.6). We read this under the structural lens of Theorem 3.7: PACS shifts mix abduction shift (which CRO is built for) with partial shifts in the deduction map—rendering style on a sketch is not only a confounder for what’s depicted but also a partial determinant of fYf_{Y} (silhouettes that work as a sketch read as a different category as a photo). When deduction invariance holds only approximately, the parameterized set of plausible targets is a worse cover of the true target, and the worst-case-optimal predictor trades headroom against caution. PACS therefore reads as a robustness check rather than as a setting where CRO’s structural assumptions cleanly apply.

Source vs. target risk on PACS.

Figure 6 is the PACS analog of Figure 3: source-validation risk vs. held-out target risk across CRO checkpoints, one color per held-out domain. The picture is qualitatively different from Colored MNIST. Source risk concentrates in a narrow 0.020.02–0.050.05 band across all cells—the featurizer fits the three source domains tightly—while target risk varies over a much wider band (roughly 0.020.02 to 0.340.34) depending on the held-out domain. The held-out-domain identity dominates the spread: Photo as target sits below y=xy{=}x at ≈0.03\approx 0.03 target risk because real photographs are closer to the average of the other three source mixes; Sketch as target sits highest at ≈0.15\approx 0.15–0.300.30 because abstract line drawings depart most from photographic priors. At fixed source risk, target risk varies by ∼\sim0.20.2 within a cell, so source-validation selection is much less informative on PACS than on the Colored MNIST source-tracking cells—consistent with the deduction-shift reading of the cross-domain behavior on PACS.

OfficeHome.

OfficeHome (Venkateswara et al., 2017) contains 65 categories across 4 domains (Art, Clipart, Product, Real). Table 6 reports leave-one-domain-out test accuracy under the standard DomainBed protocol.

CRO leads the OfficeHome average (69.369.3 vs. CORAL 68.768.7, Mixup/SagNet 68.168.1) and tops three of the four cells (Clipart, Product, Real); on Art, CORAL leads by 0.50.5 points (65.365.3 vs. 64.864.8). The 6565-class structure of OfficeHome spreads the abduction signal across many fine-grained categories, so the per-domain prior πs​(U~)\pi_{s}(\tilde{U}) that CRO models is rich enough to give a meaningful adversary search space without entering the over-parameterized regime of Figure 4; the structural assumption (deduction invariance) is also a closer fit than on PACS, because the four OfficeHome domains differ primarily in image style rather than in what is being depicted.

5.4 Empirical validation of the structural premises

To check that the structural conditions underlying CRO are simultaneously satisfiable on a real estimator stack—rather than to argue that they hold in nature—we construct a moral-questions DGP in the spirit of the running example, and report four diagnostics tied to Assumptions 3.3, 3.5 and 3.6. The SCM in Assumption 3.1 is fixed by construction here (we choose the data-generating mechanism); the diagnostics below test whether the parameterized factorization closes empirically on ϕ⁡(X)\phi(X), whether per-domain abduction maps actually differ, whether the deduction map is invariant across domains, and whether a transplant basis LL exists.

Construction.

Each record has unobserved moral values UU coarsened to a triple U~∈{−1,0,+1}3\tilde{U}\in\{-1,0,+1\}^{3} (|𝒰~|=27|\tilde{\mathcal{U}}|=27) along the three axes of Table 1; XX is one of the 680680 high-ambiguity binary-choice ethical scenarios from MoralChoice (Scherrer et al., 2023); Y∈{A,B}Y\in\{A,B\} is the chosen action elicited from claude-haiku-4-5-20251001, frozen, under a values-conditioned prompt encoding U~\tilde{U}. Three domains share the scenario library, the topic-conditional P⁡(topic∣U~)P(\text{topic}\mid\tilde{U}), and the response mechanism P⁡(Y∣X,U~)P(Y\mid X,\tilde{U}), and differ only in the per-axis moral-values prior πs​(U~)\pi_{s}(\tilde{U}) (Table 2). On the pooled 42,00042{,}000-record set (14,00014{,}000/domain) we fit the abduction map AsA_{s} by per-domain multinomial logistic regression of U~\tilde{U} on ϕ⁡(X)\phi(X), and the deduction map DD by per-u~\tilde{u} binary logistic regression of YY on ϕ⁡(X)\phi(X) pooled across all domains, with ϕ⁡(X)=RoBERTa​-​base​CLS​(X)\phi(X)=\mathrm{RoBERTa\text{-}base\;CLS}(X) (Liu et al., 2019).

Factorization closure.

Table 7 reports per-domain quality of the factorized prediction P^s​(y1∣x)=softmax​(As⊤​ϕ​(x))⊤​sigmoid​(D⊤​ϕ​(x))\widehat{P}^{s}(y_{1}\mid x)=\mathrm{softmax}(A_{s}^{\top}\phi(x))^{\top}\mathrm{sigmoid}(D^{\top}\phi(x)) against the empirical labels and against an unconstrained binary logistic regression X→YX\to Y. Calibration is exact to three decimals across all three domains and the per-record probability correlation with direct LR is 0.930.93–0.960.96. The accuracy gap to direct LR ranges from 00 pp on Pragmatist (factorized == direct =0.809=0.809) to ≈5\approx 5 pp on Idealist and Centrist, the price of constraining the predictor to the abduction–deduction factorization rather than letting it be an unconstrained black box.

Domain shift in abduction subspaces.

The abduction maps AsA_{s} have stable rank ≈15\approx 15 across domains and are positioned distinctly in column space. Table 8 reports pairwise principal angles between col⁡(As)\mathrm{col}(A_{s}) and col⁡(As′)\mathrm{col}(A_{s^{\prime}}). The median ∼\sim65∘65^{\circ} is stable across data scales (same numbers at N=2,000N=2{,}000 and N=14,000N=14{,}000 per domain), so the spread is a property of the data-generating process rather than sample noise: the three abduction maps carve out distinct preferred directions, giving the adversary three meaningfully separated “corners” to interpolate among.

Deduction invariance.

When a (s,u~)(s,\tilde{u}) cell has enough samples to estimate the per-domain deduction column Ds[:,u~]D_{s}[:,\tilde{u}] cleanly, it matches the pooled D[:,u~]D[:,\tilde{u}] to column-cosine 1.0001.000. The median column-cosine across all valid columns is dragged down (≈0.69\approx 0.69–0.720.72) only by sparsely-sampled cells where the per-domain LR is dominated by L2L_{2} regularization rather than data, sharpening to near-11 as NN grows—consistent with sample-size noise rather than genuine domain-dependence in DD. Deduction invariance (Assumption 3.3) holds.

Existence of a transplant basis LL.

We seek L∈ℝd×rL\in\R^{d\times r} satisfying As⊤​L=IrA_{s}^{\top}L=I_{r} for s∈{prag,ideal,cent,⋆}s\in\{\text{prag},\text{ideal},\text{cent},\star\} and D⊤​L=0D^{\top}L=0 simultaneously, with the Hausdorff penalty controlling where the transplant lands relative to source-pool support. Table 9 sweeps the penalty weight λH\lambda_{H}. The biorthogonality residual sits at the rank-deficiency floor (≈1\approx 1 per AA, driven by a single rare cell with n=6n=6 records), independent of λH\lambda_{H}; DD-orthogonality is achieved at machine epsilon (‖D⊤​L‖F<5×10−4\|D^{\top}L\|_{F}<5\times 10^{-4}) across the sweep. Increasing λH\lambda_{H} shrinks the Hausdorff term from 998998 to 377377 at modest cost in biorthogonality, mapping out a clean trade-off curve. LL exists across the full sweep, so Assumption 3.6 is non-vacuous on this DGP.

Summary.

Across the four diagnostics: (i) the abduction–deduction factorization closes empirically (calibration exact, 8989–91%91\% argmax-agreement with direct LR), (ii) abduction maps are domain-distinct (median ∼\sim65∘65^{\circ} pairwise principal angles), (iii) deduction invariance holds (per-domain DsD_{s} matches pooled DD to cosine 1.0001.000 in well-sampled cells), and (iv) a transplant basis LL exists at the rank-deficiency floor with DD-orthogonality essentially free and a clean Hausdorff trade-off. The structural premises that CRO assumes are simultaneously satisfiable on the empirical estimators, with all residuals consistent with finite-sample noise. We emphasize the scope of this conclusion: the moral-questions DGP is constructed so that the structural premises hold by design, and these diagnostics show that the estimator stack recovers them rather than that the premises hold in nature; the experiment is a self-consistency check on the parameterization, not evidence that the same premises hold on PACS, OfficeHome, or other real-world benchmarks.

6 Conclusion

Target risk under an unseen distribution is not pinned down by source data: many abduction–deduction factorizations are consistent with the same source-trained predictor (the abduction–deduction entanglement, Equation 3), and they disagree about how predictions shift under regime change. Representation transplant—a class of low-rank linear operations on a frozen pretrained representation—turns this entanglement into a parameterization. The headline use, presented in Section 2, is multi-domain generalization: under deduction invariance and closure under transplant, a learner–adversary game (CRO; Section 3) attains best worst-case target risk over the parameterized set of plausible target distributions, with invariant representations recovered as a corollary (Corollary 2.5). On the diagnostic Colored MNIST cell the resulting classifier holds up where established baselines collapse; on the real-world PACS and OfficeHome benchmarks, where deduction invariance is only approximately satisfied, CRO is competitive with the strongest baselines (leading on OfficeHome and matching the broad baseline cluster on PACS). A separately constructed moral-questions DGP (Section 5.4) checks that the structural conditions CRO leans on are simultaneously satisfiable on real estimators, with residuals consistent with sample noise. In short: representation transplant gives a small, structured parameterization of abduction–deduction non-identifiability on top of a frozen pretrained representation, and the CRO algorithm built on it attains minimax-optimal worst-case target risk under the structural assumptions of Section 3.

Limitations.

The closure assumption (Assumption 3.6) is the load-bearing condition throughout the paper. It plays a role analogous to positivity/coverage in standard causal inference and is closely connected to disentanglement assumptions in causal representation learning (Schölkopf et al., 2021; Locatello et al., 2019; von Kügelgen et al., 2021; Ahuja et al., 2023); it is not directly testable from observational data, and its empirical enforcement is via penalty (Equation 17) on source pairs only. Closure to the target regime is assumed, not enforced. Deduction invariance (Assumption 3.3) is a sharper assumption than it may appear: real-world shifts often mix abduction shift with partial shifts in fYf_{Y} itself (e.g., rendering style on PACS is not purely a confounder), so the parameterized set of plausible targets is a tight cover only when the structural match-up holds. This is reflected empirically: CRO’s headroom is largest on Colored MNIST, where the assumption matches the data-generating process by construction, and shrinks on real-world benchmarks where the match-up is approximate. The minimax-optimality result of Theorem 3.7 additionally requires infinite source data and global convergence of the gradient-based searches inside CRO; Theorem 3.10 and Proposition 3.11 relax these to a linear O⁡(ϵ)O(\epsilon) degradation under approximate closure and a O⁡(1/N)O(1/\sqrt{N}) statistical plug-in error, but tight finite-sample constants for the softmax/sigmoid-linear-in-ϕ\phi parameterization are left to future work.

Outlook.

The construction in this paper is best read as a way to parameterize causal models on top of pretrained foundation representations. Two directions follow naturally. Sequence models and causal structure among tokens. The setup here treats XX as a single input with a representation ϕ⁡(X)\phi(X). Lifting it to sequence models—where the causal relationships sit among the tokens themselves and can carry richer structure than a single confounder U~\tilde{U}—opens partial-transportability questions to language modeling and other sequential domains. Supervised domain adaptation via transplant fine-tuning. When a small labeled target sample is available, the same abduction–deduction parameterization admits a different statistical regime: rather than retraining (ϕ,h)(\phi,h) on the target, one can fix ϕ\phi and fit the transplant parameters ({A~s},L~)(\{\tilde{A}_{s}\},\tilde{L}) jointly to source and target data, with potential statistical advantages over full target re-training. This is mechanically related to the parameter-efficient finetuning regime of ReFT (Wu et al., 2024); the new content here is that the optimized parameters carry a causal-structural meaning (an abduction–deduction factorization), so the same operator family also delivers a transportability guarantee rather than just an empirical adaptation. The relative statistical efficiency of transplant-fine-tuning vs. full target re-training is an open question.
