Appendix A Proofs

This appendix gives formal statements and proofs for the claims in Sections 2 and 3. We work throughout under the parameterizations eqs. 6 and 7 as exact identities (writing “==” rather than “≈\approx”); approximation error from finite-rank representation fits propagates linearly through every identity below.

A.1 Existence of a transplant basis

The cross-domain transplant operator (Definition 2.4) requires a matrix L∈ℝd×rL\in\R^{d\times r} that simultaneously left-inverts every abduction map and lies in the left-null-space of the deduction map. The next proposition characterizes when such an LL exists.

Proposition A.1 (Existence of a transplant basis).

Let A1,…,AK,A⋆,D∈ℝd×rA_{1},\dots,A_{K},A_{\star},D\in\R^{d\times r} and let M:=[A1⋯AKA⋆D]∈ℝd×(K+2)​rM:=[A_{1}\;\cdots\;A_{K}\;\;A_{\star}\;\;D]\in\R^{d\times(K+2)r}. The system

As⊤L=Ir∀s∈{1,…,K,⋆},D⊤L=0,A_{s}^{\top}L=I_{r}\;\;\forall s\in\{1,\dots,K,\star\},\qquad D^{\top}L=0, (25)

admits a solution L∈ℝd×rL\in\R^{d\times r} if and only if the following kernel condition holds: every (a1,…,aK,a⋆,c)∈ℝr×⋯×ℝr(a_{1},\dots,a_{K},a_{\star},c)\in\R^{r}\times\cdots\times\R^{r} with ∑s=1KAs​as+A⋆​a⋆+D​c=0\sum_{s=1}^{K}A_{s}a_{s}+A_{\star}a_{\star}+Dc=0 satisfies ∑s=1Kas+a⋆=0\sum_{s=1}^{K}a_{s}+a_{\star}=0. A sufficient condition is rank⁡(M)=(K+2)​r\rank(M)=(K+2)r: the columns of [A1⋯AKA⋆D][A_{1}\;\cdots\;A_{K}\;A_{\star}\;D] are jointly linearly independent. The dimension constraint d≥(K+2)​rd\geq(K+2)r is necessary for rank⁡(M)=(K+2)​r\rank(M)=(K+2)r but not sufficient—under d≥(K+2)​rd\geq(K+2)r the rank attains its maximum at generic-position parameters and can fail to do so at non-generic ones (e.g. overlapping column spans of {As,D}\{A_{s},D\}). When the kernel condition holds and rank⁡(M)<d\rank(M)<d, the solution set is an affine subspace of ℝd×r\R^{d\times r} of dimension r⁡(d−rank⁡(M))r\,(d-\rank(M)).

Proof.

Stack L=[ℓ1,…,ℓr]∈ℝd×rL=[\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{r}]\in\R^{d\times r} column by column. The constraints in eq. 25 read, for each j∈{1,…,r}j\in\{1,\dots,r\},

M⊤​ℓj=tj,tj:=[ejej0r]∈ℝ(K+2)​r,M^{\top}\ell_{j}=t_{j},\qquad t_{j}:=\begin{bmatrix}e_{j}\\ \vdots\\ e_{j}\\ 0_{r}\end{bmatrix}\in\R^{(K+2)r},

where eje_{j} denotes the jj-th canonical basis vector of ℝr\R^{r}, appearing in the K+1K+1 abduction blocks and zero in the deduction block. By the fundamental theorem of linear algebra, M⊤​ℓj=tjM^{\top}\ell_{j}=t_{j} has a solution iff tj∈range⁡(M⊤)=(ker⁡M)⟂t_{j}\in\range(M^{\top})=(\ker M)^{\perp}, equivalently ⟨tj,z⟩=0\langle t_{j},z\rangle=0 for every z∈ker⁡Mz\in\ker M. Writing z=(a1,…,aK,a⋆,c)z=(a_{1},\dots,a_{K},a_{\star},c),

⟨tj,z⟩=∑s=1Kej⊤​as+ej⊤​a⋆+0r⊤​c=∑s=1Kas,j+a⋆,j,\langle t_{j},z\rangle=\sum_{s=1}^{K}e_{j}^{\top}a_{s}+e_{j}^{\top}a_{\star}+0_{r}^{\top}c=\sum_{s=1}^{K}a_{s,j}+a_{\star,j},

so the condition is ∑s=1Kas+a⋆=0\sum_{s=1}^{K}a_{s}+a_{\star}=0. The sufficient condition rank⁡(M)=(K+2)​r\rank(M)=(K+2)r implies ker⁡M={0}\ker M=\{0\}, in which case the constraint is vacuous. The dimension count follows from dimrange⁡(M⊤)=rank⁡(M)\dim\range(M^{\top})=\rank(M) and the fact that the solution set of M⊤​ℓj=tjM^{\top}\ell_{j}=t_{j} is an affine (d−rank⁡(M))(d-\rank(M))-dimensional translate of ker⁡(M⊤)\ker(M^{\top}). Table 9 reports empirical feasibility for K=3K=3 at the rank-deficiency floor. ∎

Remark A.2 (Underdetermination and the role of the Hausdorff penalty).

When rank⁡(M)<d\rank(M)<d, the solution set of eq. 25 is an affine subspace of dimension r⁡(d−rank⁡(M))r\,(d-\rank(M)). The Hausdorff penalty in eq. 17 selects a specific element of this affine subspace—the parameterization treats LL as a free parameter and uses the Hausdorff term to anchor the transplanted representations near the empirical source supports.

A.2 Action of the transplant operator on abduction/deduction readouts

Lemma A.3 (Action of Ts→s′T_{s\to s^{\prime}} on the readouts).

Under Assumptions 3.5 and 3.6, for every s,s′∈{1,…,K,⋆}s,s^{\prime}\in\{1,\dots,K,\star\} and every W∈ℝdW\in\R^{d},

As′⊤​Ts→s′​W=As⊤​W,D⊤​Ts→s′​W=D⊤​W.A_{s^{\prime}}^{\top}T_{s\to s^{\prime}}W=A_{s}^{\top}W,\qquad D^{\top}T_{s\to s^{\prime}}W=D^{\top}W. (26)

By Definition 2.4, Ts→s′=Id+L⁡(As⊤−As′⊤)T_{s\to s^{\prime}}=I_{d}+L(A_{s}^{\top}-A_{s^{\prime}}^{\top}). Using As′⊤​L=As⊤​L=IrA_{s^{\prime}}^{\top}L=A_{s}^{\top}L=I_{r} and D⊤​L=0D^{\top}L=0,

A.3 Invariant representation: proof of Corollary 2.5

We first state the distributional-match condition in formal terms; Section 2.4 introduces it informally.

Assumption A.4 (Distributional match across domains).

Let LL satisfy Assumption 3.6 and pick any A∈ℝd×rA\in\R^{d\times r} with A⊤​L=IrA^{\top}L=I_{r} (e.g. A=AsA=A_{s} for any s∈{1,…,K,⋆}s\in\{1,\dots,K,\star\} works under Assumption 3.6). Decompose

ϕ⁡(X)=W=WA+WD,WA:=L​A⊤​ϕ​(X),WD:=(Id−L​A⊤)​ϕ​(X).\phi(X)=W=W_{A}+W_{D},\qquad W_{A}:=LA^{\top}\phi(X),\quad W_{D}:=(I_{d}-LA^{\top})\phi(X).

For every s,s′∈{1,…,K,⋆}s,s^{\prime}\in\{1,\dots,K,\star\} and every wD∈range⁡(Id−L​A⊤)w_{D}\in\range(I_{d}-LA^{\top}), the conditional distribution of WAW_{A} given WD=wDW_{D}=w_{D} in domain ss matches the pushforward under Ts→s′T_{s\to s^{\prime}} of the corresponding conditional in domain s′s^{\prime}:

Ps​(WA∣WD=wD)=(Ts→s′)#​Ps′​(WA∣WD=wD),P^{s}\!\big(W_{A}\mid W_{D}=w_{D}\big)\;=\;(T_{s\to s^{\prime}})_{\#}\,P^{s^{\prime}}\!\big(W_{A}\mid W_{D}=w_{D}\big),

viewing Ts→s′T_{s\to s^{\prime}} as a linear bijection of ℝd\R^{d} (Lemma A.3) restricted to the appropriate fibers. Under Assumption 3.2 the relevant measures are discrete on ϕ⁡(𝒳)⊂ℝd\phi(\mathcal{X})\subset\R^{d}, and the pushforward is the relabeling of finite-support point masses induced by Ts→s′T_{s\to s^{\prime}}.

Remark A.5 (Ts→s′T_{s\to s^{\prime}} preserves the deduction component).

Since Ts→s′−Id=L⁡(As⊤−As′⊤)T_{s\to s^{\prime}}-I_{d}=L(A_{s}^{\top}-A_{s^{\prime}}^{\top}) takes values in range⁡(L)\range(L), which is annihilated by Id−L​A⊤I_{d}-LA^{\top}, the operator Ts→s′T_{s\to s^{\prime}} leaves WDW_{D} invariant: (Id−L​A⊤)​Ts→s′​w=(Id−L​A⊤)​w(I_{d}-LA^{\top})T_{s\to s^{\prime}}w=(I_{d}-LA^{\top})w for all ww. Consequently Ts→s′T_{s\to s^{\prime}} restricts to a bijection of each WAW_{A}-fiber {wD+wA:wA∈range⁡(L)}\{w_{D}+w_{A}:w_{A}\in\range(L)\}, acting on the wAw_{A}-coordinate as the affine map wA↦wA+L⁡(As⊤−As′⊤)​(wD+wA)w_{A}\mapsto w_{A}+L(A_{s}^{\top}-A_{s^{\prime}}^{\top})(w_{D}+w_{A}). The linear part of this restriction equals (I+L⁡(As⊤−As′⊤))|range⁡(L)=I|range⁡(L)\bigl(I+L(A_{s}^{\top}-A_{s^{\prime}}^{\top})\bigr)|_{\range(L)}=I|_{\range(L)} (using As⊤​L=As′⊤​L=IrA_{s}^{\top}L=A_{s^{\prime}}^{\top}L=I_{r}), so the fiberwise restriction is a translation of range⁡(L)\range(L) — a bijection of the WAW_{A}-fiber. Under Assumption 3.2 the pushforward in Assumption A.4 is the relabeling of the discrete WAW_{A}-mass at fixed WD=wDW_{D}=w_{D} induced by this bijection.

Proof of Corollary 2.5.

Fix s,s′∈{1,…,K,⋆}s,s^{\prime}\in\{1,\dots,K,\star\} and wD∈range⁡(Id−L​A⊤)w_{D}\in\range(I_{d}-LA^{\top}). By the law of total probability (and Assumption 3.2, so the integral is a sum over the discrete WAW_{A}-fiber at WD=wDW_{D}=w_{D}),

Ps​(y1∣WD=wD)=∑wAPs​(y1∣W=wD+wA)​Ps​(wA∣wD).P^{s}(y_{1}\mid W_{D}=w_{D})=\sum_{w_{A}}P^{s}(y_{1}\mid W=w_{D}+w_{A})\,P^{s}(w_{A}\mid w_{D}). (27)

By Assumption 3.6, for ϕ\phi-almost every w=wD+wAw=w_{D}+w_{A} in suppPs⁡(ϕ)\supp_{P^{s}}(\phi) the transplanted vector Ts→s′​wT_{s\to s^{\prime}}w lies in suppPs′⁡(ϕ)\supp_{P^{s^{\prime}}}(\phi); combining the abduction–deduction entanglement eq. 4 for both domains with the parameterizations eqs. 6 and 7 and Lemma A.3,

Ps​(y1∣W=w)\displaystyle P^{s}(y_{1}\mid W=w) =softmax​(As⊤​w)⊤​sigmoid​(D⊤​w)\displaystyle=\mathrm{softmax}(A_{s}^{\top}w)^{\top}\mathrm{sigmoid}(D^{\top}w)
=softmax​(As′⊤​Ts→s′​w)⊤​sigmoid​(D⊤​Ts→s′​w)=Ps′​(y1∣W=Ts→s′​w),\displaystyle=\mathrm{softmax}(A_{s^{\prime}}^{\top}T_{s\to s^{\prime}}w)^{\top}\mathrm{sigmoid}(D^{\top}T_{s\to s^{\prime}}w)=P^{s^{\prime}}(y_{1}\mid W=T_{s\to s^{\prime}}w),

so the summand in eq. 27 satisfies Ps​(y1∣W=wD+wA)=Ps′​(y1∣W=Ts→s′​(wD+wA))P^{s}(y_{1}\mid W=w_{D}+w_{A})=P^{s^{\prime}}(y_{1}\mid W=T_{s\to s^{\prime}}(w_{D}+w_{A})). Substituting and applying Assumption A.4 as a relabeling on the (finite) WAW_{A}-fiber,

Ps​(y1∣WD=wD)\displaystyle P^{s}(y_{1}\mid W_{D}=w_{D}) =∑wAPs′​(y1∣W=Ts→s′​(wD+wA))​Ps​(wA∣wD)\displaystyle=\sum_{w_{A}}P^{s^{\prime}}\!\big(y_{1}\mid W=T_{s\to s^{\prime}}(w_{D}+w_{A})\big)\,P^{s}(w_{A}\mid w_{D})
=∑wA′Ps′​(y1∣W=wD+wA′)​Ps′​(wA′∣wD)\displaystyle=\sum_{w_{A}^{\prime}}P^{s^{\prime}}\!\big(y_{1}\mid W=w_{D}+w_{A}^{\prime}\big)\,P^{s^{\prime}}(w_{A}^{\prime}\mid w_{D})
=Ps′​(y1∣WD=wD).∎\displaystyle=P^{s^{\prime}}(y_{1}\mid W_{D}=w_{D}).\qed

A.4 Formal definition of the plausible target set

Theorem 3.7 ranges over the set 𝒫⋆​(P1,…,PK)\mathcal{P}^{\star}(P^{1},\dots,P^{K}) of target distributions entailed by the source distributions and the structural assumptions Assumptions 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.5 and 3.6.

Definition A.6 (Plausible target set).

Fix source distributions P1,…,PKP^{1},\dots,P^{K} on 𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y} and a frozen representation ϕ:𝒳→ℝd\phi:\mathcal{X}\to\R^{d}. The plausible target set entailed by P1,…,PKP^{1},\dots,P^{K} is

𝒫⋆​(P1,…,PK):={P~⋆∈𝒫⁡(𝒳×𝒴):∃(A~1,…,A~K,A~⋆,D~,L~)∈Θ​ such that ​Π​(θ~,P1,…,PK,P~⋆)​ holds},\mathcal{P}^{\star}(P^{1},\dots,P^{K}):=\Big\{\,\tilde{P}^{\star}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y})\;:\;\exists\,(\tilde{A}_{1},\dots,\tilde{A}_{K},\tilde{A}_{\star},\tilde{D},\tilde{L})\in\Theta\text{ such that }\,\Pi(\tilde{\theta};P^{1},\dots,P^{K},\tilde{P}^{\star})\text{ holds}\,\Big\}, (28)

where Θ\Theta is the parameter domain and Π\Pi collects the structural constraints, defined as follows:

  1. (P1)

    (Domain and norm bound.) A~s,D~,L~∈ℝd×r\tilde{A}_{s},\tilde{D},\tilde{L}\in\R^{d\times r} for every s∈{1,…,K,⋆}s\in\{1,\dots,K,\star\}, with operator norms bounded by a fixed constant BB: ‖A~s‖op,‖D~‖op,‖L~‖op≤B\|\tilde{A}_{s}\|_{\mathrm{op}},\|\tilde{D}\|_{\mathrm{op}},\|\tilde{L}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq B. The empirical analog of this bound is the operator-norm penalty controlled by cro_lambda_op (see Table 10); the softmax/sigmoid parameterizations eqs. 6 and 7 are invariant under translating A~s\tilde{A}_{s} by 𝟙r⁡u⊤\1_{r}u^{\top} for any u∈ℝdu\in\R^{d} (a softmax gauge), so the bound is imposed after fixing this gauge (e.g., zero-mean columns of A~s\tilde{A}_{s}).

  2. (P2)

    (Linear abduction.) The transplant dimension is identified with the coarsening support size, r=|𝒰~|r=|\tilde{\mathcal{U}}|; for every x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} and every s∈{1,…,K,⋆}s\in\{1,\dots,K,\star\},

    P~→s​(𝒖~∣x):=softmax⁡(A~s⊤​ϕ​(x))∈ℝr,\vec{\tilde{P}}^{s}(\bm{\tilde{u}}\mid x)\;:=\;\mathrm{softmax}(\tilde{A}_{s}^{\top}\phi(x))\;\in\;\R^{r},

    read as a probability vector indexed by u~∈𝒰~\tilde{u}\in\tilde{\mathcal{U}} in a fixed ordering (Assumption 3.5).

  3. (P3)

    (Invariant deduction.) D~∈ℝd×r\tilde{D}\in\R^{d\times r} does not depend on ss; for every x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} and every u~∈𝒰~\tilde{u}\in\tilde{\mathcal{U}},

    P~​(y1∣x,u~):=[sigmoid⁡(D~⊤​ϕ​(x))]u~,\tilde{P}(y_{1}\mid x,\tilde{u})\;:=\;\bigl[\mathrm{sigmoid}(\tilde{D}^{\top}\phi(x))\bigr]_{\tilde{u}},

    the u~\tilde{u}-th entry of the sigmoid output, read as a conditional probability (Assumption 3.3).

  4. (P4)

    (Source-fit.) For every s∈{1,…,K}s\in\{1,\dots,K\} and every x∈suppPs⁡(X)x\in\supp_{P^{s}}(X),

    Ps​(y1∣x)=softmax​(A~s⊤​ϕ​(x))⊤​sigmoid​(D~⊤​ϕ​(x)).P^{s}(y_{1}\mid x)\;=\;\mathrm{softmax}(\tilde{A}_{s}^{\top}\phi(x))^{\top}\,\mathrm{sigmoid}(\tilde{D}^{\top}\phi(x)).
  5. (P5)

    (Biorthogonality.) A~s⊤​L~=Ir\tilde{A}_{s}^{\top}\tilde{L}=I_{r} for every s∈{1,…,K,⋆}s\in\{1,\dots,K,\star\} and D~⊤​L~=0\tilde{D}^{\top}\tilde{L}=0 (Assumption 3.6).

  6. (P6)

    (Closure.) For every s,s′∈{1,…,K,⋆}s,s^{\prime}\in\{1,\dots,K,\star\} and every w∈ℝdw\in\R^{d}, Ps​(ϕ⁡(X)=w)>0⇔Ps′​(ϕ⁡(X)=T~s→s′​w)>0P^{s}(\phi(X)=w)>0\iff P^{s^{\prime}}(\phi(X)=\tilde{T}_{s\to s^{\prime}}w)>0, where T~s→s′:=Id+L~​(A~s⊤−A~s′⊤)\tilde{T}_{s\to s^{\prime}}:=I_{d}+\tilde{L}(\tilde{A}_{s}^{\top}-\tilde{A}_{s^{\prime}}^{\top}) (Assumption 3.6).

  7. (P7)

    (Target consistency.) The marginal P~⋆​(X)\tilde{P}^{\star}(X) has suppP~⋆⁡(X)=suppP⋆⁡(X)\supp_{\tilde{P}^{\star}}(X)=\supp_{P^{\star}}(X), and the conditional satisfies P~⋆​(y1∣x)=softmax​(A~⋆⊤​ϕ​(x))⊤​sigmoid​(D~⊤​ϕ​(x))\tilde{P}^{\star}(y_{1}\mid x)=\mathrm{softmax}(\tilde{A}_{\star}^{\top}\phi(x))^{\top}\,\mathrm{sigmoid}(\tilde{D}^{\top}\phi(x)) for every x∈suppP~⋆⁡(X)x\in\supp_{\tilde{P}^{\star}}(X).

Conditions (P1)–(P3) and (P5)–(P6) are the structural assumptions of Assumptions 3.5, 3.3 and 3.6; (P4) imposes that the parameterization fits the source distributions; (P7) defines the candidate target distribution from the parameters. (P4) together with the abduction–deduction entanglement eq. 4 pins the inner product A~s⊤​ϕ​(x)⋅D~⊤​ϕ​(x)\tilde{A}_{s}^{\top}\phi(x)\cdot\tilde{D}^{\top}\phi(x) to the source prediction Ps​(y1∣x)P^{s}(y_{1}\mid x) but leaves the individual factors underdetermined—this is the multi-domain abduction–deduction entanglement.

Remark A.7 (Empirical version).

Definition A.6 uses populations PsP^{s}. With finite samples, Algorithm 1 works with empirical P^s\hat{P}^{s}, and (P4) is enforced by the source-fit penalty Fit\mathrm{Fit} in eq. 18 with weight λ1\lambda_{1}; (P6) is enforced by the Hausdorff penalty Closure\mathrm{Closure} in eq. 17 with weight λ2\lambda_{2}. As λ1,λ2→∞\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}\to\infty the empirical adversary’s feasible set converges to the plausible set 𝒫⋆​(P^1,…,P^K)\mathcal{P}^{\star}(\hat{P}^{1},\dots,\hat{P}^{K}) in Definition A.6 with the empirical distributions in (P4)–(P6).

A.5 Target-side consistency identity

Proposition A.8 (Target consistency).

Under Assumptions 3.1, 3.3, 3.5 and 3.6, for every s′∈{1,…,K}s^{\prime}\in\{1,\dots,K\} and every x0⋆∈𝒳x_{0}^{\star}\in\mathcal{X} with P⋆​(ϕ⁡(X)=ϕ⁡(x0⋆))>0P^{\star}(\phi(X)=\phi(x_{0}^{\star}))>0,

P⋆​(y1∣X=x0⋆)=Ps′​(y1∣X∈ϕ−1​(T⋆→s′​ϕ​(x0⋆))).P^{\star}(y_{1}\mid X=x_{0}^{\star})=P^{s^{\prime}}\!\big(y_{1}\mid X\in\phi^{-1}(T_{\star\to s^{\prime}}\,\phi(x_{0}^{\star}))\big). (29)

This is eq. 16 in the body.

Proof.

Fix s′∈{1,…,K}s^{\prime}\in\{1,\dots,K\} and x0⋆∈𝒳x_{0}^{\star}\in\mathcal{X} with P⋆​(ϕ⁡(X)=ϕ⁡(x0⋆))>0P^{\star}(\phi(X)=\phi(x_{0}^{\star}))>0. Write T:=T⋆→s′T:=T_{\star\to s^{\prime}} and w:=ϕ⁡(x0⋆)w:=\phi(x_{0}^{\star}). By Assumption 3.6 applied to {⋆,s′}\{\star,s^{\prime}\}, there exists x′∈𝒳x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X} with ϕ⁡(x′)=T​w\phi(x^{\prime})=Tw and Ps′​(ϕ⁡(X)=ϕ⁡(x′))>0P^{s^{\prime}}(\phi(X)=\phi(x^{\prime}))>0. Under Assumptions 3.5 and 3.3, Ps′​(y1∣x)P^{s^{\prime}}(y_{1}\mid x) depends on xx only through ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) (both the abduction parameterization softmax⁡(As′⊤​ϕ​(x))\mathrm{softmax}(A_{s^{\prime}}^{\top}\phi(x)) and the deduction parameterization sigmoid⁡(D⊤​ϕ​(x))\mathrm{sigmoid}(D^{\top}\phi(x)) are functions of ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) alone), so Ps′​(y1∣x)P^{s^{\prime}}(y_{1}\mid x) is constant on ϕ\phi-fibers and Ps′​(y1∣X∈ϕ−1​(T​w))=Ps′​(y1∣x′)P^{s^{\prime}}(y_{1}\mid X\in\phi^{-1}(Tw))=P^{s^{\prime}}(y_{1}\mid x^{\prime}) for any representative x′∈ϕ−1​(T​w)∩suppPs′⁡(X)x^{\prime}\in\phi^{-1}(Tw)\cap\supp_{P^{s^{\prime}}}(X). Combining the abduction–deduction entanglement eq. 4 for Ps′P^{s^{\prime}} at x′x^{\prime} with the parameterizations eqs. 6 and 7,

Ps′​(y1∣x′)\displaystyle P^{s^{\prime}}(y_{1}\mid x^{\prime}) =softmax​(As′⊤​T​w)⊤​sigmoid​(D⊤​T​w)=softmax​(A⋆⊤​w)⊤​sigmoid​(D⊤​w),\displaystyle=\mathrm{softmax}(A_{s^{\prime}}^{\top}Tw)^{\top}\mathrm{sigmoid}(D^{\top}Tw)=\mathrm{softmax}(A_{\star}^{\top}w)^{\top}\mathrm{sigmoid}(D^{\top}w),

where the second equality is Lemma A.3. Applying eq. 4 for P⋆P^{\star} at x0⋆x_{0}^{\star} together with the target abduction parameterization softmax⁡(A⋆⊤​ϕ​(x))=P→⋆​(𝒖~∣x)\mathrm{softmax}(A_{\star}^{\top}\phi(x))=\vec{P}^{\star}(\bm{\tilde{u}}\mid x) and the shared (invariant) deduction parameterization sigmoid⁡(D⊤​ϕ​(x))=P→⋆​(y1∣x,𝒖~)\mathrm{sigmoid}(D^{\top}\phi(x))=\vec{P}^{\star}(y_{1}\mid x,\bm{\tilde{u}}), the right-hand side equals P⋆​(y1∣x0⋆)P^{\star}(y_{1}\mid x_{0}^{\star}). Hence P⋆​(y1∣x0⋆)=Ps′​(y1∣x′)P^{\star}(y_{1}\mid x_{0}^{\star})=P^{s^{\prime}}(y_{1}\mid x^{\prime}), which is eq. 29. ∎

A.6 Proof of theorem 3.7

The proof has three steps. First, the target consistency identity (Proposition A.8) ties the unobserved target to the sources. Second, we identify the adversary’s optimal solution set with 𝒫⋆​(P1,…,PK)\mathcal{P}^{\star}(P^{1},\dots,P^{K}) from Definition A.6. Third, we invoke the min-max convergence statement of Theorem A.9 below to conclude that the learner’s iterates converge to the minimax optimum over 𝒫⋆\mathcal{P}^{\star}.

Proof of Theorem 3.7.

Step 1 (Target consistency). By Proposition A.8, for every s′∈{1,…,K}s^{\prime}\in\{1,\dots,K\} and every x0⋆∈suppP⋆⁡(X)x_{0}^{\star}\in\supp_{P^{\star}}(X), eq. 29 holds: the unobserved target P⋆​(Y∣X)P^{\star}(Y\mid X) at any in-support point equals a transplant of an observed source conditional.

Step 2 (Plausible-set characterization.) Define

ℱ⁡(P1,…,PK):={(g~⋆,{A~s}s=1K,A~⋆,D~,L~):(P1)–(P6) hold}\mathcal{F}(P^{1},\dots,P^{K}):=\Big\{\,(\tilde{g}^{\star},\{\tilde{A}_{s}\}_{s=1}^{K},\tilde{A}_{\star},\tilde{D},\tilde{L})\;:\;\text{(P1)--(P6) hold}\,\Big\}

and recall from Definition A.6 that each θ~∈ℱ\tilde{\theta}\in\mathcal{F} induces a candidate target distribution P~⋆​(θ~)\tilde{P}^{\star}(\tilde{\theta}) via (P7). We claim

{P~⋆​(θ~):θ~∈ℱ⁡(P1,…,PK)}=𝒫⋆​(P1,…,PK),\big\{\tilde{P}^{\star}(\tilde{\theta}):\tilde{\theta}\in\mathcal{F}(P^{1},\dots,P^{K})\big\}=\mathcal{P}^{\star}(P^{1},\dots,P^{K}),

i.e., the parameter family ranged over by the adversary in line 4 of Algorithm 1 (in the limit λ1,λ2→∞\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}\to\infty) is exactly the plausible target set of Definition A.6. The inclusion “⊆\subseteq” is by construction. For “⊇\supseteq”, let P~⋆∈𝒫⋆\tilde{P}^{\star}\in\mathcal{P}^{\star} and let θ~=(A~1,…,A~K,A~⋆,D~,L~)\tilde{\theta}=(\tilde{A}_{1},\dots,\tilde{A}_{K},\tilde{A}_{\star},\tilde{D},\tilde{L}) be the witness in Definition A.6; this witness satisfies (P7), which requires Assumption 3.6 to hold at s′=⋆s^{\prime}=\star—i.e., target-side closure is assumed, not constructed. Setting g~⋆​(W):=softmax​(A~⋆⊤​W)⊤​sigmoid​(D~⊤​W)\tilde{g}^{\star}(W):=\mathrm{softmax}(\tilde{A}_{\star}^{\top}W)^{\top}\mathrm{sigmoid}(\tilde{D}^{\top}W) gives a feasible point with P~⋆​(θ~)=P~⋆\tilde{P}^{\star}(\tilde{\theta})=\tilde{P}^{\star} through (P7). The empirical adversary in line 4 enforces (P4)–(P6) at the sources but cannot enforce (P7); target-side closure is the load-bearing assumption that lets the source-only witness extend to a target-side one.

Step 3 (Min-max convergence.) Under Assumption 3.2, the surrogate target risk P~⋆↦RP~⋆​(h)\tilde{P}^{\star}\mapsto R_{\tilde{P}^{\star}}(h) is continuous, and for each P~⋆\tilde{P}^{\star} the map h↦RP~⋆​(h)h\mapsto R_{\tilde{P}^{\star}}(h) is convex. Here “ℋ\mathcal{H} is a convex function class” is meant in the function-space sense: ℋ\mathcal{H} is a set of [0,1][0,1]-valued classification heads closed under finite convex combinations, λ​h1+(1−λ)​h2∈ℋ\lambda h_{1}+(1-\lambda)h_{2}\in\mathcal{H} for h1,h2∈ℋ,λ∈[0,1]h_{1},h_{2}\in\mathcal{H},\lambda\in[0,1]. The running loss ℓ\ell is the convex surrogate cross-entropy (Section 1), which is pointwise convex in the predicted probability p^=h⁡(x)\hat{p}=h(x); combined with ℋ\mathcal{H} closed under convex combinations and the surrogate evaluated on the finite support of Assumption 3.2, this gives convexity of h↦RP~⋆​(h)h\mapsto R_{\tilde{P}^{\star}}(h) by pointwise propagation. (No restriction to a particular parameterization of ℋ\mathcal{H}, e.g., linear-in-ϕ\phi, is required; non-convex parametric families such as deep nets fit this framework via their convex hull, equivalently stochastic mixtures.) The parameter space

ΘB:={(A~1,…,A~K,A~⋆,D~,L~)∈(ℝd×r)K+3:(P1)–(P6) hold}\Theta_{B}:=\Big\{(\tilde{A}_{1},\dots,\tilde{A}_{K},\tilde{A}_{\star},\tilde{D},\tilde{L})\in(\R^{d\times r})^{K+3}\;:\;\text{(P1)--(P6) hold}\Big\}

is bounded by the operator-norm constraint in (P1) and closed by the polynomial equality constraints in (P2)–(P6) (the support condition (P6) is closed because XX has finite support by Assumption 3.2), hence compact in the finite-dimensional ambient space. The plausible set 𝒫⋆​(P1,…,PK)\mathcal{P}^{\star}(P^{1},\dots,P^{K}) is the image of ΘB\Theta_{B} under the continuous parameter-to-distribution map θ~↦P~⋆​(θ~)\tilde{\theta}\mapsto\tilde{P}^{\star}(\tilde{\theta}) defined by (P7), hence compact. The hypotheses of Theorem A.9 therefore hold. Applying that theorem with adversary oracle (line 4 of Algorithm 1) and learner oracle (line 6) gives Mt→V⋆:=minh∈ℋ⁡maxP~⋆∈𝒫⋆​RP~⋆​(h)M_{t}\to V^{\star}:=\min_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\max_{\tilde{P}^{\star}\in\mathcal{P}^{\star}}R_{\tilde{P}^{\star}}(h) as t→∞t\to\infty. By the lower-bound-at-the-limit step of Theorem A.9, the worst-case risk of iterate hth_{t} satisfies maxP~⋆∈𝒫⋆⁡RP~⋆​(ht)≤Mt+1\max_{\tilde{P}^{\star}\in\mathcal{P}^{\star}}R_{\tilde{P}^{\star}}(h_{t})\leq M_{t+1}. For the lower bound: since ht∈ℋh_{t}\in\mathcal{H} is one specific element of ℋ\mathcal{H}, its worst-case risk is at least the infimum of worst-case risks over ℋ\mathcal{H} — that is,

maxP~⋆∈𝒫⋆⁡RP~⋆​(ht)≥infh∈ℋmaxP~⋆∈𝒫⋆⁡RP~⋆​(h)=V⋆,\max_{\tilde{P}^{\star}\in\mathcal{P}^{\star}}R_{\tilde{P}^{\star}}(h_{t})\;\geq\;\inf_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\max_{\tilde{P}^{\star}\in\mathcal{P}^{\star}}R_{\tilde{P}^{\star}}(h)\;=\;V^{\star},

which is a definitional consequence of V⋆V^{\star} being the minimax value and does not require the convergence we are establishing. Sandwiching gives

V⋆≤maxP~⋆∈𝒫⋆⁡RP~⋆​(ht)≤Mt+1→t→∞V⋆.V^{\star}\;\leq\;\max_{\tilde{P}^{\star}\in\mathcal{P}^{\star}}R_{\tilde{P}^{\star}}(h_{t})\;\leq\;M_{t+1}\;\xrightarrow{t\to\infty}\;V^{\star}.

Termination triggers as ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0 at t=t⁡(ϵ)→∞t=t(\epsilon)\to\infty, so maxP~⋆∈𝒫⋆⁡RP~⋆​(h⋆)→V⋆\max_{\tilde{P}^{\star}\in\mathcal{P}^{\star}}R_{\tilde{P}^{\star}}(h^{\star})\to V^{\star} as ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0, which is the conclusion of Theorem 3.7. The argmax over the plausible set 𝒫⋆\mathcal{P}^{\star} corresponds to the worst-case target distribution entailed by (K+1)(K+1)-tuples of SCMs compatible with Assumptions 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.5 and 3.6. ∎

A.7 Min-max game and convergence

The CRO algorithm (Algorithm 1) is an instance of an iterative learner–adversary min-max game: at iteration tt, the adversary supplies a risk-maximizing distribution P^t⋆∈𝒫⋆\hat{P}^{\star}_{t}\in\mathcal{P}^{\star}, the learner solves a minimax problem on the growing collection 𝒫^t⋆={P^1⋆,…,P^t⋆}\hat{\mathcal{P}}^{\star}_{t}=\{\hat{P}^{\star}_{1},\dots,\hat{P}^{\star}_{t}\}, and the procedure terminates when the learner’s worst-case risk on 𝒫^t⋆\hat{\mathcal{P}}^{\star}_{t} stops increasing. The convergence statement below was invoked in Step 3 of the proof of Theorem 3.7; the argument follows the structure of Jalaldoust et al. (2024, Appendix C), adapted to the transplant-parameterized adversary.

Theorem A.9 (Min-max convergence).

Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be a compact set of probability distributions on 𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}, let ℋ\mathcal{H} be a convex hypothesis class, and let ℓ\ell be a loss with h↦RP​(h)h\mapsto R_{P}(h) convex and P↦RP​(h)P\mapsto R_{P}(h) continuous. Consider the iteration: starting from 𝒫^0=∅\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{0}=\emptyset and any h0∈ℋh_{0}\in\mathcal{H}, for t≥1t\geq 1 set

Pt∈arg​maxP∈𝒫⁡RP​(ht−1),𝒫^t:=𝒫^t−1∪{Pt},ht∈arg​minh∈ℋ⁡maxP∈𝒫^t​RP​(h),P_{t}\in\argmax_{P\in\mathcal{P}}R_{P}(h_{t-1}),\qquad\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{t}:=\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{t-1}\cup\{P_{t}\},\qquad h_{t}\in\argmin_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\,\max_{P\in\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{t}}R_{P}(h),

and let Mt:=maxP∈𝒫^t⁡RP​(ht)M_{t}:=\max_{P\in\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{t}}R_{P}(h_{t}). Assume each argmax/argmin attains its global optimum. Then MtM_{t} is non-decreasing in tt, and

limt→∞Mt=minh∈ℋ⁡maxP∈𝒫​RP​(h).\lim_{t\to\infty}M_{t}\;=\;\min_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\,\max_{P\in\mathcal{P}}R_{P}(h).

For every ϵ>0\epsilon>0, the stopping rule |Mt−Mt−1|≤ϵ|M_{t}-M_{t-1}|\leq\epsilon triggers in finitely many iterations, and MtM_{t} at termination is within ϵ\epsilon of the minimax value.

Proof sketch.

Monotonicity. At round tt, 𝒫^t⊇𝒫^t−1\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{t}\supseteq\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{t-1}, so Mt=minh⁡maxP∈𝒫^t​RP​(h)≥minh⁡maxP∈𝒫^t−1​RP​(h)=Mt−1M_{t}=\min_{h}\max_{P\in\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{t}}R_{P}(h)\geq\min_{h}\max_{P\in\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{t-1}}R_{P}(h)=M_{t-1} (the inner max over a larger set is no smaller). Hence Mt≥Mt−1M_{t}\geq M_{t-1}.

Boundedness. Mt≤maxP∈𝒫⁡RP​(ht)≤suph,PRP​(h)<∞M_{t}\leq\max_{P\in\mathcal{P}}R_{P}(h_{t})\leq\sup_{h,P}R_{P}(h)<\infty by compactness and continuity. So MtM_{t} converges to some M∞M_{\infty}.

Lower bound at the limit. By construction Mt+1≥maxP∈𝒫^t+1⁡RP​(ht+1)≥RPt+1​(ht)=maxP∈𝒫⁡RP​(ht)M_{t+1}\geq\max_{P\in\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{t+1}}R_{P}(h_{t+1})\geq R_{P_{t+1}}(h_{t})=\max_{P\in\mathcal{P}}R_{P}(h_{t}), so M∞≥lim inft→∞maxP∈𝒫⁡RP​(ht)≥minh⁡maxP∈𝒫​RP​(h)M_{\infty}\geq\liminf_{t\to\infty}\max_{P\in\mathcal{P}}R_{P}(h_{t})\geq\min_{h}\max_{P\in\mathcal{P}}R_{P}(h).

Upper bound at the limit. Mt=minh∈ℋ⁡maxP∈𝒫^t​RP​(h)≤minh⁡maxP∈𝒫​RP​(h)M_{t}=\min_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\max_{P\in\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{t}}R_{P}(h)\leq\min_{h}\max_{P\in\mathcal{P}}R_{P}(h) since 𝒫^t⊆𝒫\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{P}. Together, M∞=minh⁡maxP∈𝒫​RP​(h)M_{\infty}=\min_{h}\max_{P\in\mathcal{P}}R_{P}(h), the minimax value.

Finite termination. The increasing bounded sequence MtM_{t} has |Mt−Mt−1|→0|M_{t}-M_{t-1}|\to 0, so any positive tolerance ϵ\epsilon is eventually achieved. ∎

Remark A.10 (Application in CRO).

Theorem A.9 applies with 𝒫=𝒫⋆​(P1,…,PK)\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}^{\star}(P^{1},\dots,P^{K}) (Definition A.6). The algorithm itself manipulates the empirical plausible set 𝒫^⋆\hat{\mathcal{P}}^{\star} constructed from P^1,…,P^K\hat{P}^{1},\dots,\hat{P}^{K}; under the infinite-source-data hypothesis of Theorem 3.7, the empirical source distributions coincide with the population PsP^{s} and the empirical plausible set coincides with 𝒫⋆\mathcal{P}^{\star}, so the convergence target V⋆V^{\star} is the population minimax value over 𝒫⋆\mathcal{P}^{\star}. The adversary oracle in line 4 of Algorithm 1 approximates arg​maxP∈𝒫⋆⁡RP​(ht−1)\argmax_{P\in\mathcal{P}^{\star}}R_{P}(h_{t-1}) by gradient ascent on Obj^\hat{\mathrm{Obj}} over the parameters (g~⋆,{A~s},L~)(\tilde{g}^{\star},\{\tilde{A}_{s}\},\tilde{L}); under the “each gradient-based search attains its global optimum” hypothesis of Theorem 3.7 the oracle is exact. The learner oracle in line 6 solves minh∈ℋ⁡maxP∈𝒫^⋆​RP​(h)\min_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\max_{P\in\hat{\mathcal{P}}^{\star}}R_{P}(h) over the finite collection 𝒫^⋆\hat{\mathcal{P}}^{\star}, which is a standard finite-domain minimax problem.

A.8 Robustness and finite-sample bounds

This subsection proves the two robustness statements from Section 3.3: Theorem 3.10 (graceful degradation under approximate closure) and Proposition 3.11 (finite-sample plug-in error). The plausible target set 𝒫ϵ⋆\mathcal{P}^{\star}_{\epsilon} under the ϵ\epsilon-relaxed closure of Definition 3.9 is defined exactly as in Definition A.6, with condition (P6) replaced by its ϵ\epsilon-relaxed analog: for every s,s′∈{1,…,K,⋆}s,s^{\prime}\in\{1,\dots,K,\star\} and every ww in suppPs⁡(ϕ⁡(X))\supp_{P^{s}}(\phi(X)), there exists w′∈suppPs′⁡(ϕ⁡(X))w^{\prime}\in\supp_{P^{s^{\prime}}}(\phi(X)) with ‖w′−T~s→s′​w‖≤ϵ\|w^{\prime}-\tilde{T}_{s\to s^{\prime}}w\|\leq\epsilon (and symmetrically).

A.8.1 Proof of Theorem 3.10

We split the bound into two steps: a coupling step that shows every P~⋆∈𝒫ϵ⋆\tilde{P}^{\star}\in\mathcal{P}^{\star}_{\epsilon} admits a partner P~0⋆∈𝒫0⋆\tilde{P}^{\star}_{0}\in\mathcal{P}^{\star}_{0} within W1W_{1}-distance ϵ\epsilon, and a stability step that propagates the coupling to the risk.

Step 1: Coupling. Let P~⋆∈𝒫ϵ⋆\tilde{P}^{\star}\in\mathcal{P}^{\star}_{\epsilon} with witness (A~1,…,A~K,A~⋆,D~,L~)(\tilde{A}_{1},\dots,\tilde{A}_{K},\tilde{A}_{\star},\tilde{D},\tilde{L}). Define P~0⋆∈𝒫0⋆\tilde{P}^{\star}_{0}\in\mathcal{P}^{\star}_{0} as the distribution that, for each transplanted source representation T~s→⋆ϕ(x)\tilde{T}_{s\to\star}\phi(x), snaps to the closest target-support point ϕ⁡(x′)\phi(x^{\prime}) with ∥ϕ(x′)−T~s→⋆ϕ(x)∥≤ϵ\|\phi(x^{\prime})-\tilde{T}_{s\to\star}\phi(x)\|\leq\epsilon (which exists by ϵ\epsilon-relaxed closure), with mass preserved. Under Assumption 3.2 both distributions are discrete with finite support; the snapping induces a deterministic mass-preserving rearrangement of P~⋆\tilde{P}^{\star} onto P~0⋆\tilde{P}^{\star}_{0} in which each atom moves by at most ϵ\epsilon, so

W1​(P~⋆,P~0⋆)≤ϵ.W_{1}(\tilde{P}^{\star},\tilde{P}^{\star}_{0})\;\leq\;\epsilon.

Step 2: Stability. The hypothesis that h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H} is LhL_{h}-Lipschitz with values in [δ,1−δ][\delta,1-\delta] gives, for cross-entropy ℓ⁡(p^,y)=−log⁡p^y\ell(\hat{p},y)=-\log\hat{p}_{y},

|ℓ⁡(h⁡(w),y)−ℓ⁡(h⁡(w′),y)|≤1δ|h⁡(w)−h⁡(w′)|≤Lhδ​‖w−w′‖,|\ell(h(w),y)-\ell(h(w^{\prime}),y)|\;\leq\;\frac{1}{\delta}\,|h(w)-h(w^{\prime})|\;\leq\;\frac{L_{h}}{\delta}\|w-w^{\prime}\|,

so w↦ℓ⁡(h⁡(w),y)w\mapsto\ell(h(w),y) is (Lh/δ)(L_{h}/\delta)-Lipschitz for each fixed yy. By Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality on the discrete support,

|RP~⋆​(h)−RP~0⋆​(h)|≤Lhδ⋅W1​(P~⋆,P~0⋆)≤Lhδ⋅ϵ.|R_{\tilde{P}^{\star}}(h)-R_{\tilde{P}^{\star}_{0}}(h)|\;\leq\;\frac{L_{h}}{\delta}\cdot W_{1}(\tilde{P}^{\star},\tilde{P}^{\star}_{0})\;\leq\;\frac{L_{h}}{\delta}\cdot\epsilon.

Taking the supremum over P~⋆∈𝒫ϵ⋆\tilde{P}^{\star}\in\mathcal{P}^{\star}_{\epsilon} and the corresponding P~0⋆∈𝒫0⋆\tilde{P}^{\star}_{0}\in\mathcal{P}^{\star}_{0},

supP~⋆∈𝒫ϵ⋆RP~⋆​(h)≤supP~0⋆∈𝒫0⋆RP~0⋆​(h)+Lhδ​ϵ,\sup_{\tilde{P}^{\star}\in\mathcal{P}^{\star}_{\epsilon}}R_{\tilde{P}^{\star}}(h)\;\leq\;\sup_{\tilde{P}^{\star}_{0}\in\mathcal{P}^{\star}_{0}}R_{\tilde{P}^{\star}_{0}}(h)\;+\;\frac{L_{h}}{\delta}\,\epsilon,

and taking minh\min_{h} on both sides yields Vϵ⋆≤V0⋆+(Lh/δ)​ϵV^{\star}_{\epsilon}\leq V^{\star}_{0}+(L_{h}/\delta)\epsilon. The lower bound Vϵ⋆≥V0⋆V^{\star}_{\epsilon}\geq V^{\star}_{0} is immediate from 𝒫0⋆⊆𝒫ϵ⋆\mathcal{P}^{\star}_{0}\subseteq\mathcal{P}^{\star}_{\epsilon}. □\square

A.8.2 Sketch of Proposition 3.11

We give the decomposition; tight bracketing-entropy constants for the softmax/sigmoid-linear-in-ϕ\phi class are standard and out of scope for this paper.

Write V^:=minh∈ℋ⁡maxP^∈𝒫^⋆​RP^​(h)\widehat{V}:=\min_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\max_{\hat{P}\in\hat{\mathcal{P}}^{\star}}R_{\hat{P}}(h) for the empirical minimax value attained by Algorithm 1 in the exact-oracle setting, and decompose

maxP~⋆∈𝒫⋆⁡RP~⋆​(h^)=V0⋆+[maxP~⋆∈𝒫⋆⁡RP~⋆​(h^)−V^]⏟(a)​ statistical+[V^−V0⋆]⏟(b)​ approx. + closure.\max_{\tilde{P}^{\star}\in\mathcal{P}^{\star}}R_{\tilde{P}^{\star}}(\hat{h})\;=\;V^{\star}_{0}\;+\;\underbrace{\bigl[\max_{\tilde{P}^{\star}\in\mathcal{P}^{\star}}R_{\tilde{P}^{\star}}(\hat{h})-\widehat{V}\bigr]}_{(\mathrm{a})\text{ statistical}}\;+\;\underbrace{\bigl[\widehat{V}-V^{\star}_{0}\bigr]}_{(\mathrm{b})\text{ approx.\ + closure}}.

Term (a) bounds the population worst case of the empirical minimizer by the empirical worst case at the same head; by Step 3 of the Theorem 3.7 proof the parameter space ΘB\Theta_{B} in (P1) is compact in operator norm, and the parameter-to-distribution map θ~↦P~⋆​(θ~)\tilde{\theta}\mapsto\tilde{P}^{\star}(\tilde{\theta}) is continuous. A uniform-convergence argument over ΘB\Theta_{B} at scale η\eta then gives, with probability 1−δ1-\delta,

supθ~∈ΘB|RP⋆​(θ~)​(h^)−RP^⋆​(θ~)​(h^)|≤C1​log⁡𝒩⁡(ΘB,η)+log⁡(1/δ)N+η,\sup_{\tilde{\theta}\in\Theta_{B}}|R_{P^{\star}(\tilde{\theta})}(\hat{h})-R_{\hat{P}^{\star}(\tilde{\theta})}(\hat{h})|\;\leq\;C_{1}\sqrt{\frac{\log\mathcal{N}(\Theta_{B},\eta)+\log(1/\delta)}{N}}\;+\;\eta,

where C1C_{1} depends on the cross-entropy Lipschitz constant 1/δ1/\delta from Theorem 3.10 and the operator-norm bound BB. Term (b) decomposes further into the optimization gap ϵopt\epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}} of the inner adversary/learner searches relative to their global optima (this is zero under the oracle hypothesis of Theorem 3.7, and quantified by the gradient-method analyses cited there in practice), and the empirical Hausdorff residual ϵHaus=Closure⁡(A^s,L^)\epsilon_{\mathrm{Haus}}=\mathrm{Closure}(\hat{A}_{s},\hat{L}) which contributes to the gap between the empirical plausible set 𝒫^⋆\hat{\mathcal{P}}^{\star} and its population counterpart 𝒫⋆\mathcal{P}^{\star} via the same W1W_{1}-coupling argument as in Theorem 3.10. Combining gives eq. 24. The bracketing-entropy bound for softmax/sigmoid-linear-in-ϕ\phi heads with explicit constants (e.g. via standard arguments for VC-major classes or covering numbers of bounded linear maps) is orthogonal to the paper’s contribution and left to future work. □\square

Appendix B Experimental details

We document the implementation, training procedure, hyperparameter search, datasets, compute, and reproducibility protocol for CRO. Settings not noted here follow the DomainBed defaults of Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz (2021).

B.1 Codebase and framework

CRO is implemented on top of the DomainBed framework (Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz, 2021), registered as a new Algorithm subclass alongside ERM and the baselines reported in our tables. We preserve DomainBed’s sweep protocol, dataset loaders, train/holdout splits, and model-selection criteria.

B.2 Architectures

Image datasets (PACS, OfficeHome).

The featurizer ϕ\phi is ResNet-50 pretrained on ImageNet with AugMix (timm checkpoint resnet50.ram_in1k). BatchNorm parameters are frozen during both training phases. The final classification head hh is reinitialized as a single linear layer on top of ϕ\phi.

MNIST-style datasets (Colored MNIST).

The featurizer is the standard 4-layer convolutional MNIST_CNN used by DomainBed.

Inputs and augmentation.

Image inputs are resized to 224×224224\times 224 with ImageNet mean/std normalization. Training-time augmentation: RandomResizedCrop(224, scale=(0.7,1.0)), RandomHorizontalFlip, ColorJitter(0.3,0.3,0.3,0.3), and RandomGrayscale. No augmentation on Colored MNIST beyond DomainBed defaults.

B.3 Two-phase training

CRO training proceeds in two phases.

Phase 1 — pretrain.

Standard ERM-style training of the (ϕ,h)(\phi,h) pair on the union of source domains: 5000 SGD steps for image datasets, 500 steps for Colored MNIST. Phase-1 checkpoints are cached on disk keyed by (dataset,test_envs,trial_seed)(\text{dataset},\,\text{test\_envs},\,\text{trial\_seed}); subsequent hyperparameter samples within a sweep reuse the same checkpoint, so the pretrain cost is paid once per (dataset, test environment, trial). Phase-1 learning rate, batch size, and weight decay are fixed (not sampled) to enable cache hits: LR 5×10−55\times 10^{-5} (image) or 10−310^{-3} (MNIST), batch size 3232 (image) or 6464 (MNIST), weight decay 00.

Phase 2 — CRO refinement.

The adversary g~⋆\tilde{g}^{\star} is initialized as a copy of the Phase-1 head hh. The outer loop of Algorithm 1 alternates: (i) update the adversary using the transplant-dimension-rr reparameterized operator (parameters ({A~s},L~)(\{\tilde{A}_{s}\},\tilde{L})); (ii) update the learner hh. Termination is when the running gap of the worst-case risk drops below ϵgap\epsilon_{\text{gap}} (sampled as cro_gap_eps) or cro_max_outer_iters is reached. Each outer iteration runs a fixed number of inner adversary and learner epochs (sampled per-dataset; see Table 11).

B.4 Hyperparameter search and model selection

For each dataset and each held-out test environment we sample 20 hyperparameter configurations ×\times 3 trial seeds, yielding 240240 runs per 4-domain benchmark (180 for 3-domain Colored MNIST). All jobs use DomainBed’s --single_test_envs mode (one held-out target per run). Model selection follows the DomainBed default: the best hyperparameter configuration per cell is picked using training-domain validation accuracy only, so target labels are never observed during selection.

Table 10 reports the search ranges (log-uniform unless noted), and Table 11 reports per-dataset Phase-2 compute ranges, chosen so the total Phase-2 work is comparable across datasets of different scales.

B.5 Datasets

B.6 Compute

All experiments run on a shared workstation with 8 ×\times NVIDIA H100 (80 GB). Each benchmark uses 2 GPUs in parallel with up to 4 jobs per GPU (8 concurrent slots), with per-job memory 77–1212 GB. Datasets and Phase-1 caches are staged in a /dev/shm RAM tier to remove disk I/O as a bottleneck on the shared box; per-process thread caps (OMP_NUM_THREADS=16, TORCH_NUM_THREADS=16) prevent CPU oversubscription.

Per-job wall-clock: < 1<\,1 min on Colored MNIST, ∼10{\sim}10–1515 min on PACS, ∼20{\sim}20 min on OfficeHome.

B.7 Reproducibility

Trial seeds are {0,1,2}\{0,1,2\}, paired with hyperparameter seeds drawn from DomainBed’s standard sweep. The per-job random seed is a deterministic function of

(dataset,algorithm,test_env,trial_seed,hp_seed)(\text{dataset},\,\text{algorithm},\,\text{test\_env},\,\text{trial\_seed},\,\text{hp\_seed})

, so any individual run reproduces from those five identifiers. The Phase-1 pretrain cache is keyed by (dataset,test_envs,trial_seed)(\text{dataset},\,\text{test\_envs},\,\text{trial\_seed}) and produces bit-identical checkpoints under repeated runs, isolating Phase-2 variation. The hyperparameter ranges (Tables 10 and 11), search procedure, and DomainBed sweep configuration above are sufficient to reproduce the reported numbers up to seed-level variance.
